q: What has Canada's national pharmacare program actually delivered since the Pharmacare Act passed in 2024: which provinces and territories have signed agreements, what is covered, how many people are using it, and what do the Parliamentary Budget Officer and other independent estimates say the full program would cost?

sentences.sentence: Section 6(1) reads: "6 (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes." [4] The obligation on the Minister is triggered by the existence of an agreement, not by residence in Canada.

Section 6(2): "For greater certainty, any agreement referred to in subsection (1) with a province or territory is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients." [4] First-dollar coverage means no deductible and no co-payment at the pharmacy counter for the covered products — the federal contribution is not a subsidy layered on top of an existing provincial deductible scheme but a requirement that the covered items cost the patient nothing.

Section 3 states that the Act's purpose "is to guide efforts to improve, for all Canadians, the accessibility and affordability of prescription drugs and related products, and to support their appropriate use, in collaboration with the provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders, with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare." [4] The operative phrase is "continuing to work toward." The Act commits the federal government to a direction of travel, not to a delivered universal program.

Section 4 then lists the principles the Minister "is to consider" when collaborating — consistent coverage, affordability, appropriate use and universal coverage — alongside the Canada Health Act. [4]

Health Canada's contraception backgrounder described the intended basket as including "oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, injections, implants, rings, and morning-after pills" — a list put forward for discussion with provinces and territories, so that the effective scope of coverage in any given province is fixed by the bilateral agreement, not by the Act. [6]

Further details regarding this fund will be provided following discussions with PT partners, who will be essential partners to its roll out." [5] The device fund was thus an intention announced alongside the legislation, not an entitlement created by it, and its details were left to negotiations that had not yet happened when the bill passed.

All four signed within a five-week window in early 2025, and Health Canada's bilateral agreements page — updated 26 January 2026 — still described the count as four: "The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free." [12] That leaves nine provinces and two territories without an agreement roughly eighteen months after royal assent, including Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Saskatchewan and the two northern territories other than Yukon.

The four, in signing order: **Manitoba — 27 February 2025.** The first agreement, announced as "this first-ever national pharmacare agreement," with "more than $219 million over four years." [14] The agreement's own schedule sets Stream 1 transfers of $52,509,230 in 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each of the following three years, plus a one-time $9,945,348 in Stream 2 device funding in 2025-26 [8] — the schedule behind the "more than $219 million" headline [14].

Manitoba's implementation date in the agreement text was 15 April 2025, although the signing release told residents to expect coverage "for the majority of these products in June 2025." [14] Manitoba was therefore the first jurisdiction where the benefit actually existed at a pharmacy counter. **British Columbia — 6 March 2025.** The largest agreement: "more than $670 million over four years," covering contraceptives, diabetes medications, devices and supplies. [13]
Stream 1 payments are $17,406,567 in 2025-26, then $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29; a one-time Stream 2 payment of $37,839,549 arrives in 2026-27 [7].
That schedule is the basis of the "more than $670 million" in the signing release [13].

The fiscal profile is unusual and revealing: BC's first-year transfer is $17,406,567 against $204,948,289 in each later year, about a twelfth, because its implementation date was set for 1 March 2026. [7]

As a condition of the deal, BC also agreed to add free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms from 1 March 2026, a benefit outside the Act's two categories and funded by the province. [13] **Prince Edward Island — 7 March 2025.** "More than $30 million over four years." [15] The schedule gives $6,795,833 in 2025-26 and $7,404,416 in each of the next three years, plus $1,188,243 one-time for devices [10] — the "more than $30 million" headline [15].

PEI's implementation date was 1 May 2025, making it the second jurisdiction live. [10] **Yukon — 20 March 2025.** "Up to $9.5 million over four years." [16] Stream 1 transfers are $2,548,410 in 2026-27 and $2,650,056 in each of 2027-28 and 2028-29, plus $306,143 one-time for devices [9] — a schedule that begins only in 2026-27 and sits below the "up to $9.5 million" headline [16].

Yukon's implementation date in the agreement is "between April 15 and May 5, 2026" [9], which contradicts the signing release's promise that "Yukon residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products no later than January 2026." [16] On the agreement's own text, Yukoners were covered more than a year after their government signed, and three to four months later than the federal announcement said. **The pattern in the dates is the finding.** Signing an agreement and delivering a benefit are separate events, separated by between one and fourteen months.

Second, the published headline figures do not add up to the first-phase envelope usually described as $1.5 billion: more than $670 million for BC [13], more than $219 million for Manitoba [14], more than $30 million for PEI [15] and up to $9.5 million for Yukon [16] leave a large remainder unallocated.

What a patient gets is narrower than "free birth control and diabetes drugs," and the qualifications are documented on the government's own pages rather than in commentary. **The basket is a negotiated list, not a category.** Coverage runs to "a range of birth control options and diabetes medications" and applies to the products listed in each agreement's Annex A. [21]

That means the basket can differ between jurisdictions and can be extended by negotiation — which is exactly what BC did, adding free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms from 1 March 2026 as part of its deal, a benefit outside the Act's two categories and funded by the province rather than the federal transfer. [13] **First-dollar coverage applies to the drug and the dispensing fee — not to everything at the counter.** Health Canada's page is precise: pharmacare "only covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee" and it will not cover delivery fees or pharmacist prescribing fees. [21]

The bilateral agreements page adds the same caveat in softer language, saying products "will be available for free or at low cost at the pharmacy counter" and that "Other fees, such as prescribing fees or delivery fees, may still apply." [12] Two consequences follow.

Second, the statutory "first-dollar coverage" guarantee in section 6(2) of the Act [4] covers the drug; it does not reach the professional fees around it, so the "no cost to patients" claim is true of the product and not of the transaction. **There is no deductible and no co-payment on the covered products, and private insurance is bypassed rather than coordinated.** The bilateral agreements page tells patients: "You **won't** need to coordinate benefits with private insurance plans." [12] This is a design choice with real effects: a person with employer drug coverage does not submit the pharmacare claim to the private plan first, and the public plan does not act as a second payer.

The PEI agreement's clause is explicit: where the province's reported 2022-23 Stream 1 spending is greater than the amount reported elsewhere in the agreement, the agreement provides that "Canada will withhold or reduce an amount equivalent to the difference between these two amounts" [10].

Manitoba's Annex B shows how the test bites: Manitoba spent $23,195,236 on the diabetes products in the list and $750,746 on the contraceptives in 2022-23, for a total of $23,945,982 [8] — against a first-year federal transfer of $52,509,230 [8].

Federal money therefore more than doubles the provincial baseline for these products, which is the concrete meaning of "increase any existing public pharmacare coverage" in section 6(1) of the Act [4]. **What the benefit is worth to a patient is substantial and unevenly distributed.** Health Canada puts metformin at "about $100 per year," insulin at "between $900 and $1,700 per year," and sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors at "from $100 to over $1,000 per year." [2] For people with the highest costs, the federal announcement cites Diabetes Canada's 2022 finding that out-of-pocket costs ran "as high as $18,306 per year for people living with Type 1 diabetes and as high as $10,014 per year for those living with Type 2 diabetes." [13] Those figures are the upper tail — they include devices, supplies and monitoring, not just the listed drugs — but they explain why the benefit is politically salient out of proportion to its fiscal size.

A program of a few hundred million dollars a year can remove a cost of the size Diabetes Canada measured from a household with Type 1 diabetes, and that is the kind of change voters notice. **The need the program addresses is broad and was measured before it existed.** The BC announcement cites Statistics Canada's 2021 finding that "one in five adults in Canada did not have the insurance they needed to cover their medication costs." [13] That is the baseline against which the program should be judged, and it is a national figure for a program that in its first eighteen months reached four jurisdictions.

In PEI, the federal announcement made the local case directly: "Here in Prince Edward Island, residents face some of Canada's highest out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered on their public plans." [15] The provinces that signed first were not the ones with the weakest coverage on average; they were the ones whose governments chose to sign. **What is not covered matters as much as what is.** Diabetes devices and supplies sit in a separate Stream 2 fund announced outside the Act, not in the section 6 entitlement [5], and the amounts are small relative to the drug transfers — $37,839,549 for BC in 2026-27 [7], $9,945,348 for Manitoba [8], $1,188,243 for PEI [10], $306,143 for Yukon [9].

Health Canada's own page for the public is explicit that the program does not screen anyone out on the criteria that usually gate a benefit: "You're covered under pharmacare no matter your: age income private or workplace health insurance status" [3] A resident of British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island or Yukon who holds a health card is covered by operation of the bilateral agreement and the provincial plan, not by any act of registration.
In 2018, costs to the healthcare system related to diabetes were estimated at $27 billion, and they could surpass $39 billion by 2028." [2] That 3.8 million is the national denominator.

Health Canada's own summary of progress, on a page updated in January 2026, described the state of play as four agreements: "We've signed funding agreements with 4 provinces and territories to make a range of contraception (birth control) and diabetes medications free at the pharmacy counter." [2] That sentence is the federal government's own account of what has been delivered at the point of coverage — and it is a statement about agreements signed, not about prescriptions filled or patients served.

The current phase: $1.9 billion over five years.** The PBO's legislative costing note on Bill C-64 found "the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years," on the explicit assumption "that any medications that are currently covered by provincial and territorial governments, as well as private insurance providers will remain covered on the same terms." [11] The PBO's framing of the program's purpose is equally important: "The aim of the program is to expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial coverage." [20] The method is worth setting out because it determines what the number means.

The model assumes the program "will cover 100% of the expense on diabetes and contraception medication for those who currently do not have public or private drug plan coverage and for those who currently do not fill their prescriptions due to cost related reasons," with the latter group "assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions," and that it will also cover "the out-of-pocket portion of prescription costs for those who have public or private drug plan coverage." [20] In other words: for the uninsured, the program pays the whole cost; for the insured, it pays only the deductible and co-payment.

"The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage." [20] The model assumes no new federal confidential rebates, because the program's objective is to expand rather than replace existing plans — but notes that if the administrator negotiates rebates, "it will reduce the cost of the program." It excludes substitution from unlisted drugs to listed ones, which would raise cost, and it excludes savings to the Medical Expense Tax Credit.

Drug expenditure and mark-up data came from IQVIA for 2021-22, projected using Patented Medicine Prices Review Board growth rates; copper IUD costs were estimated from 2017 General Social Survey prevalence data adjusted by average IUD duration. [20] **2.
For a shorter list of essential medicines, the estimated cost in 2025 to 26 was $9.8 billion." [17] The distinction between $35 billion and $11.9 billion is the whole analytical crux.
This is the number the Committee of Experts adopted as its upper bound. [17]

We selected 5% for our lower bound estimate, while the upper bound estimate from the Parliamentary Budget Office assumes an increase of 13.5%, which is larger than estimates in the literature." [17] A 13.5% assumption for the increase in medicine use once coverage is free is at the top of the empirical range; the Committee treated that conservatism as a reason its own lower figure was defensible, not as a reason the PBO was wrong. **What the numbers mean together.** Total Canadian spending on prescribed drugs "jumped by $10 billion in 5 years – from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024." [17] Set against that $44 billion base, the full-program estimates are: $9.8 billion on an essential list (about 22% of current total spending, gross), $11.9 billion incremental on a comprehensive list, and $35 billion gross on a comprehensive list.

The enacted program is smaller than every full-program estimate by at least one order of magnitude, and smaller than the gross comprehensive estimate by nearly two. **The gap between the PBO's $1.9 billion and the money actually committed.** Budget 2024 is the source of the first-phase envelope: "Budget 2024 proposes to provide $1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2024-25, to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan." [23] That $1.5 billion sits above the PBO's $1.9 billion?

Against those two figures sit the four signed agreements: more than $670 million for BC [13], more than $219 million for Manitoba [14], more than $30 million for PEI [15] and up to $9.5 million for Yukon [16].

Documented: the PBO's five-year window starts in 2024-25, while the agreements' payment schedules begin in 2025-26 (Manitoba, PEI) or 2026-27 (Yukon), and BC's schedule front-loads only $17,406,567 in 2025-26 before rising to $204,948,289 a year [7][8][9][10].

Documented: BC's own page describes the federal contribution as "up to $670 million in funding over three years" [24], whereas Health Canada's schedule spreads payments across four fiscal years [7] — the two governments do not describe the same agreement the same way.

Its headline: "We have estimated that it will cost an additional $3.5 billion in 2022 to launch national pharmacare starting with universal coverage for essential medicines." [1] That $3.5 billion figure is a *first-step* number, covering a limited list of essential medicines, and it is routinely misquoted as the cost of pharmacare.

Overall, this would amount to a 50-55 per cent increase in public spending on prescription drugs." [1] So: PBO at $7.3 billion gross for a 2015-16 implementation, against a Council figure of $15.3 billion for 2027.

While the council’s model builds on the methodology used by the PBO, it is not identical and uses assumptions about the key drivers of prescription drug spending to project future drug costs." [1] The Council's point is that its model projects future drug costs rather than costing a program in a single year.

Scope is the second, and it is stated plainly — the PBO's $7.3 billion was for "national pharmacare... fully implemented," while the Council's $3.5 billion launch figure covers only "universal coverage for essential medicines," with the $15.3 billion arriving only "as the formulary becomes comprehensive." [1] The third difference — that the Council's figure is an increment over a provincial system assumed to keep growing — follows from the Council's own framing of its model as projecting "future drug costs" [1], and is this report's reading rather than a sentence in the report.
The PBO's $7.3 billion gross becomes $6.3 billion net of "copayment revenues and ancillary savings" [1] — a reduction of about 14 per cent.

notes.quote: We have estimated that it will cost an additional $3.5 billion in 2022 to launch national pharmacare starting with universal coverage for essential medicines.
notes.claim: The Advisory Council (Hoskins report, 2019) estimated additional public cost of $3.5B in 2022 to launch pharmacare with essential medicines, rising to $15.3B a year in 2027 as the formulary becomes comprehensive.

notes.quote: We've signed funding agreements with 4 provinces and territories to make a range of contraception (birth control) and diabetes medications free at the pharmacy counter.
notes.claim: As of Health Canada's page (updated January 2026), only four provinces/territories have pharmacare funding agreements in force — so the population that can actually use the program is limited to residents of BC, Manitoba, PEI and Yukon, not all Canadians.

notes.quote: You're covered under pharmacare no matter your: * age * income * private or workplace health insurance status
notes.claim: Coverage in a signing jurisdiction is automatic for anyone eligible for provincial health insurance — there is no separate federal enrolment or registration process, so "enrolment" in the national program is not really measured; usage has to be inferred from provincial dispensing/claims data instead.

notes.quote: About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes. In 2018, costs to the healthcare system related to diabetes were estimated at $27 billion, and they could surpass $39 billion by 2028.
notes.claim: Health Canada's own scale figure for the eligible diabetes population is about 3.8 million diagnosed people nationally — the denominator against which take-up in the four signed jurisdictions can be judged.

notes.quote: 6 (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes.
notes.claim: The Act's only operative coverage commitment is conditional: federal money flows to a province or territory only if that government signs an agreement, and only for contraception and diabetes drugs/devices, delivered as universal single-payer first-dollar coverage.

notes.quote: (2) For greater certainty, any agreement referred to in subsection (1) with a province or territory is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients.
notes.claim: The Act requires that any bilateral agreement provide first-dollar coverage — i.e. no deductibles or co-payments at the point of dispensing for the covered products (the statutory hook for the "no cost to patients" condition).

notes.quote: 3 The purpose of this Act is to guide efforts to improve, for all Canadians, the accessibility and affordability of prescription drugs and related products, and to support their appropriate use, in collaboration with the provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders, with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare.
notes.claim: The Act's purpose is to guide efforts and work "toward" national universal pharmacare — it does not itself establish a universal program; it also mandates a national formulary list and a national bulk purchasing strategy.

notes.quote: 4 The Minister is to consider the following principles and the Canada Health Act when collaborating with provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare:
notes.claim: The Act lists four principles the Minister must consider (consistent coverage, affordability, appropriate use, universal coverage) but makes them guiding considerations rather than enforceable conditions on provinces.

notes.quote: The PBO estimated that if national pharmacare had been fully implemented in 2015-16, it would have required incremental public spending of $7.3 billion ($6.3 billion net of copayment revenues and ancillary savings). Overall, this would amount to a 50-55 per cent increase in public spending on prescription drugs.
notes.claim: The Advisory Council explicitly compares its own projection with the PBO's 2017 costing: PBO found full implementation in 2015-16 would need $7.3B incremental public spending ($6.3B net of copayments/ancillary savings), a 50-55% rise in public drug spending, versus the Council's $15.3B in 2027 (~65% rise).

notes.quote: It is difficult, however, to directly compare the results of the council’s drug spending model with those of the PBO. While the council’s model builds on the methodology used by the PBO, it is not identical and uses assumptions about the key drivers of prescription drug spending to project future drug costs.
notes.claim: The Council explains why its estimate and the PBO's are not directly comparable: its model projects future drug costs (inflation, population growth and aging, new expensive drugs) and assumes provinces keep covering drugs pharmacare doesn't; but both find similar system-wide savings potential.

notes.quote: Separate from Bill C-64, the federal government is announcing its intention to establish a fund to support access to diabetes devices and supplies. Further details regarding this fund will be provided following discussions with PT partners, who will be essential partners to its roll out.
notes.claim: The diabetes drug list and device fund were announced as intentions to be negotiated with "willing provinces and territories"; the list of covered diabetes drugs was attached to a backgrounder for discussion, not written into the Act, and the diabetes devices/supplies fund is separate from Bill C-64.

notes.quote: This includes oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, injections, implants, rings, and morning-after pills.
notes.claim: The contraception list (oral pills, copper and hormonal IUDs, injections, implants, rings, emergency contraception) was a list "to be discussed with provinces and territories" — coverage depended on PT agreement, so the Act's scope is defined by negotiation, not statute.

Prince Edward Island's 2022-23 Stream 1 spending reported in _Annex B_ is greater than the amount reported under section 4.9.1.c.i.: Canada will withhold or reduce an amount equivalent to the difference between these two amounts, not exceeding the amount of funding received from Canada spent by Prince Edward Island on product costs (4.9.1.b.i.) in the Fiscal Year;
notes.claim: Each agreement permits Canada to claw back funding if the province's 2022-23 baseline spending on the same products was overstated — the mechanism by which "additionality" is enforced, i.e. federal money must add to, not replace, provincial spending.

notes.quote: Yukon's Implementation Date will be between April 15 and May 5, 2026
notes.claim: Yukon signed in March 2025 but set its implementation date for between 15 April and 5 May 2026 — free coverage began only in spring 2026, over a year after signing.

notes.quote: Prince Edward Island's Implementation Date will be May 1, 2025
notes.claim: PEI's implementation date was 1 May 2025, making it the second jurisdiction to go live after Manitoba.

notes.quote: The PBO estimates that the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years. This estimate assumes that any medications that are currently covered by provincial and territorial governments, as well as private insurance providers will remain covered on the same terms.
notes.claim: The PBO costed Bill C-64 itself at $1.9 billion over five years in incremental federal spending, explicitly assuming existing provincial/territorial and private coverage stays on the same terms — the official costing of the phase now being delivered.

notes.quote: The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free.
notes.claim: Four agreements, all signed in early 2025 (Manitoba 27 Feb, BC 6 Mar, PEI 7 Mar, Yukon 20 Mar 2025), with no further signatures as of the page's 26 January 2026 update — so nine provinces and two territories had no pharmacare agreement a year and a half after royal assent.

notes.quote: If you live in a province or territory with an agreement, those products will be available for free or at low cost at the pharmacy counter. You **won't** need to coordinate benefits with private insurance plans. Other fees, such as prescribing fees or delivery fees, may still apply.
notes.claim: Even in a signed province, "free" is qualified: the covered drug cost is covered, but prescribing fees and delivery fees may still be charged, and patients must not coordinate with private plans.

notes.quote:
As set out in the act, we have:

* received advice from a committee of experts on how to operate and finance national pharmacare
* received advice from Canada's Drug Agency on:
  * a national bulk purchasing strategy
  * a list of essential prescription drugs and related products
* published a pan-Canadian strategy to promote appropriate use of prescription drugs and related products
notes.claim: The federal government's stated post-Act deliverables are advisory and strategic, not coverage: expert committee advice, a Canada's Drug Agency bulk purchasing strategy and essential drugs list, and a pan-Canadian appropriate-use strategy.

notes.quote:
If you have diabetes and live in a province or territory with a pharmacare agreement, you'll generally have free access to medications like:

* Metformin, which can cost about $100 per year
* Insulin, which can cost between $900 and $1,700 per year
* Sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors, which can cost from $100 to over $1,000 per year
notes.claim: The order of magnitude of the drugs being made free: metformin about $100 a year, insulin $900–$1,700 a year, sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors $100 to over $1,000 a year — useful for judging what the benefit is worth to a patient.

notes.quote: Our objective is to "learn by doing" in a Canadian context. We'll base discussions about the future on what we learn as we implement existing pharmacare agreements_._
notes.claim: Health Canada describes the current phase explicitly as a learning exercise rather than a settled program: the stated objective is to "learn by doing" and to base future discussions on implementation lessons.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of more than 1.3 million British Columbians and ensure that nearly 550,000 British Columbians with diabetes can access essential medications
notes.claim: The BC agreement's own population scope: more than 1.3 million British Columbians for contraception and nearly 550,000 with diabetes — the federal government's own estimate of who the agreement reaches.

notes.quote: On April 1, 2023, the province began providing free contraceptives to all residents. In 2024 alone, approximately 227,000 people received free prescription contraception, through this nation-leading program. Since the start of the program, more than 306,000 people have benefitted.
notes.claim: BC's own free-contraception program (begun 1 April 2023, before pharmacare) gives the only published utilisation series in the country: about 227,000 people received free prescription contraception in 2024 alone, and more than 306,000 since the program started.

notes.quote: announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest more than $670 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications, devices and supplies for residents of BC.
notes.claim: BC's federal allocation is "more than $670 million over four years", and BC residents were told to expect coverage beginning March 2026 — a year after signing.

notes.quote: Through this first-ever national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $219 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for Manitobans.
notes.claim: Manitoba was the first national pharmacare agreement: more than $219 million over four years, reaching nearly 350,000 Manitobans for contraception and over 149,000 with diabetes, with coverage expected from June 2025.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of nearly 350,000 Manitobans and make sure that over 149,000 Manitobans with diabetes can access essential medications
notes.claim: Manitoba's agreement population scope: nearly 350,000 for contraception and over 149,000 people with diabetes — the smallest of the two big agreements.

notes.quote: Manitoba residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for the majority of these products in June 2025.
notes.claim: Manitoba's coverage start slipped from the June 2025 date announced at signing; the agreement text set 15 April 2025 as the implementation date, and Manitoba's own spending on the Annex A products in 2022-23 was $23.9M against $52.5M in federal money in 2025-26.

notes.quote: Through the national pharmacare agreement, the Government of Canada will provide more than $30 million over four years for universal coverage to a range of contraceptives and diabetes medications for PEI residents, at little to no direct cost to them.
notes.claim: PEI's agreement is more than $30 million over four years, reaching over 41,000 Islanders for contraception and over 16,000 with diabetes, with coverage from 1 May 2025 — the smallest province but the fastest implementation.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of over 41,000 Islanders and make sure that over 16,000 Islanders with diabetes can access essential medications
notes.claim: PEI's population reach: over 41,000 Islanders for contraception, over 16,000 for diabetes — a combined scope of roughly 57,000 people in a province of about 180,000.

notes.quote: Here in Prince Edward Island, residents face some of Canada's highest out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered on their public plans.
notes.claim: PEI's federal announcement notes Islanders "face some of Canada's highest out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered on their public plans" — the equity case for the agreement in the province with the weakest existing coverage.

notes.quote: announced the signing of a pharmacare agreement to invest up to $9.5 million over four years to provide universal access to contraceptive and diabetes medications for residents of Yukon.
notes.claim: Yukon's agreement is up to $9.5 million over four years, reaching more than 12,000 Yukoners for contraception and over 3,000 with diabetes; the signing release said coverage would begin no later than January 2026, while the agreement text sets an implementation date of 15 April to 5 May 2026 — the two dates disagree.

notes.quote: Yukon residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products no later than January 2026.
notes.claim: Yukon's release promised coverage "no later than January 2026", which the agreement text contradicts with a 15 April–5 May 2026 implementation date — a slip of several months from the public commitment.

notes.quote: This will support the reproductive freedom of more than 12,000 Yukoners and make sure that over 3,000 residents with diabetes can access essential medications
notes.claim: Yukon's population reach is small: more than 12,000 Yukoners for contraception and over 3,000 with diabetes.

notes.quote: The total cost of publicly funding a list of essential medicines will likely be between $6 to $10 billion dollars (see Appendix 2).
notes.claim: The 2025 National Pharmacare Committee of Experts estimates the total cost of publicly funding an essential medicines list at $6–10 billion a year — much lower than the Hoskins Council's comprehensive-formulary $15.3B, because the basket is a defined essential list.

notes.quote:
| Out of pocket     | 9.5        | 6.8        |
| Private Insurance | 17.3       | 12.5       |
| Public plans      | 18.8       | 13.6       |
| Pharmacare        | 0          | 8          |
notes.claim: The Committee's status-quo-versus-pharmacare table for 2025: out of pocket $9.5B falling to $6.8B, private insurance $17.3B to $12.5B, public plans $18.8B to $13.6B, with pharmacare adding $8B — the arithmetic of substitution, not pure addition.

notes.quote: Total spending on prescribed drugs in Canada jumped by $10 billion in 5 years – from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024
notes.claim: Total Canadian spending on prescribed drugs rose from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024 — the base the cost estimates are a share of.

notes.quote: This single-payer approach avoids the drawbacks of bilateral agreements, enshrines universal access and strengthens the ability to negotiate drug prices with drug companies.
notes.claim: The Committee rejects the "fill-the-gaps" model and explicitly criticises the bilateral-agreement architecture, recommending instead full federal funding of an essential medicines list delivered through health cards — a direct critique of what the 2024 Act actually built.

notes.quote: We used the 2023 report from the Parliamentary Budget Office to estimate the upper bound of the cost of pharmacare.Footnote 3Footnote 121 The estimated total cost of publicly funding a longer list of medicines (the RAMQ list from Quebec) was $35 billion in 2025 to 26\. The incremental cost to the public sector $11.9 billion. For a shorter list of essential medicines, the estimated cost in 2025 to 26 was $9.8 billion.
notes.claim: The PBO's 2023 report costed public funding of Quebec's RAMQ list at $35 billion in 2025-26, with an incremental public-sector cost of $11.9 billion; for a shorter essential medicines list the PBO figure was $9.8 billion — and the Committee adopted $9.8B as its upper bound.

notes.quote: Some studies have found no increases in use with public coverage, while others have found increases above 10%.Footnote 122Footnote 123 We selected 5% for our lower bound estimate, while the upper bound estimate from the Parliamentary Budget Office assumes an increase of 13.5%, which is larger than estimates in the literature.
notes.claim: The PBO's model assumes a 13.5% increase in medicine use once coverage is free — higher than most literature, which the Committee cites as between no increase and above 10%, and which the Committee used to argue the PBO figure is a fiscally conservative upper bound.

notes.quote: current public spending on included medicines, such as through provincial and territorial drug plans (which may account for more than 30% of the cost)
notes.claim: The Committee states plainly that its $6.0–9.8 billion estimates disregard existing provincial/territorial public spending (which "may account for more than 30% of the cost") and existing private spending — so they are gross federal costs, not increments over the status quo.

notes.quote: We used the list of 185 medicines included in the essential prescription drugs list prepared by the Canada’s Drug Agency committee to estimate the lower bound of the cost of pharmacare.
notes.claim: The 185-medicine lower-bound basket was built from Canada's Drug Agency's essential list, all off-patent and multi-source, with 2024 IQVIA dispensing data showing $12.6 billion in total spending before the savings adjustments.

notes.quote: According to the Parliamentary Budget Officer, 43% of the cost of the fill-the-gaps pharmacare plan that Bill C-64 would create as written will be financed through private insurance plans.
notes.claim: Morgan and Herder's peer-reviewed critique: the Act as written permits a fill-the-gaps model, and cites the PBO finding that 43% of the cost of the fill-the-gaps pharmacare plan Bill C-64 would create would be financed through private insurance plans.

notes.quote: An average of 13% of private health insurance premiums goes to administration, including an average profit margin of 3%.6 In contrast, the average cost of administering public drug plans in Canada — including the costs of running programs, managing formularies, negotiating prices, and processing claims — is about 1.5% of drug plan spending.
notes.claim: Administrative cost comparison that underpins the case for single payer: public drug plans cost about 1.5% of plan spending to administer, versus an average 13% of private health insurance premiums going to administration including a 3% profit margin.

notes.quote: In contrast to the fill-the-gaps approach to covering these medicines, this universal, public approach would save provincial governments $1.3 billion over the first 5 years and reduce total program costs by $1.1 billion over that period, through bulk purchasing and administrative efficiencies.
notes.claim: Morgan and Herder argued before passage that a universal public approach to just contraceptives and diabetes drugs would save provincial governments $1.3 billion over five years and reduce total program costs by $1.1 billion — i.e. the fill-the-gaps design chosen costs more than the alternative, per their modelling.

notes.quote: Estimated savings from universal public coverage of these essential medicines was $4.27 billion per year (range $2.72 billion to $5.83 billion; 28% reduction) for patients and private drug plan sponsors, at an incremental government cost of $1.23 billion per year (range $373 million to $1.98 billion; 11% reduction).
notes.claim: Morgan et al. 2017 peer-reviewed estimate: universal public coverage of a 117-drug essential medicines list would cost government an incremental $1.23 billion a year (range $373M–$1.98B) while saving patients and private plans $4.27 billion — the lowest credible cost figure for an essential-medicines approach.

notes.quote: The new program will cover 100% of the expense on diabetes and contraception medication for those who currently do not have public or private drug plan coverage and for those who currently do not fill their prescriptions due to cost related reasons. The latter group is assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions.
notes.claim: The PBO's C-64 costing method: it covers 100% of diabetes and contraception costs for the uninsured and for those who skip prescriptions on cost grounds (assumed 14% of total prescriptions), and covers the out-of-pocket portion for those already insured — i.e. top-up, not replacement.

notes.quote: The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage.
notes.claim: The PBO itself flags high uncertainty in its C-64 costing and says it is contingent on how many drugs get listed, excludes substitution effects that would raise cost, and assumes no new federal confidential rebates.

notes.quote: The aim of the program is to expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial coverage.
notes.claim: The PBO describes the Act's design intent as expanding and enhancing rather than replacing provincial coverage — the definitive official characterisation of the phase.

notes.quote:
Pharmacare covers a range of birth control options and diabetes medications. It **only** covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee. It won't cover any applicable:

* delivery fees
* pharmacist prescribing fees
notes.claim: Coverage excludes delivery fees and pharmacist prescribing fees — the drug and dispensing fee are covered, but not every cost at the counter, so "free" has an asterisk even in a signed province.

notes.quote: In 2022, Diabetes Canada determined that out-of-pocket costs were as high as $18,306 per year for people living with Type 1 diabetes and as high as $10,014 per year for those living with Type 2 diabetes.
notes.claim: The benefit's worth to a patient, per Diabetes Canada figures cited by Health Canada: out-of-pocket costs as high as $18,306 a year for Type 1 diabetes and $10,014 for Type 2 — the costs the program is meant to remove.

notes.quote: In 2021, Statistics Canada found that one in five adults in Canada did not have the insurance they needed to cover their medication costs.
notes.claim: The scale of the unmet need the program targets: in 2021 Statistics Canada found one in five Canadian adults lacked the insurance needed to cover medication costs.

notes.quote: We estimated that the incremental government cost of adding universal public coverage of the essential medicines would be $1.23 billion per year (range $373 million to $1.98 billion; 11% reduction). The incremental private sector savings from such coverage was estimated at $4.27 billion per year
notes.claim: Peer-reviewed modelling that does isolate the increment over existing public plans for an essential medicines list — the increment the section says no published estimate isolates.

notes.quote: In contrast to the fill-the-gaps approach to covering these medicines, this universal, public approach would save provincial governments $1.3 billion over the first 5 years and reduce total program costs by $1.1 billion over that period, through bulk purchasing and administrative efficiencies.
notes.claim: Morgan and Herder model exactly the phase-one medicines (contraceptives and diabetes drugs) and estimate the increment versus the fill-the-gaps design the Act permits — so the phase-one increment has been modelled, contrary to the section.

notes.quote: These agreements will support reproductive freedom by providing up to nine million women and gender diverse people in Canada free access to contraception. Additionally, the 3.7 million people in Canada living with diabetes will have universal access to a suite of medications that reduce the risk of serious health complications and improve quality of life.
notes.claim: Health Canada's own national scope figures at royal assent: up to nine million women and gender diverse people for contraception, and 3.7 million people living with diabetes — the denominators against which the four-agreement footprint can be measured.

notes.quote: Budget 2024 proposes to provide $1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2024-25, to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan.
notes.claim: Budget 2024 is the source of the first-phase envelope: $1.5 billion over five years starting 2024-25 to Health Canada, and it states the design principle that new federal funding will "expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial spending on public drug benefit programs."

notes.quote: New federal funding will expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial spending on public drug benefit programs.
notes.claim: Budget 2024 states the additionality principle in the government's own words: new federal funding "will expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial spending on public drug benefit programs," with delivery through existing provincial programs following negotiations.

notes.quote: One in four Canadians with diabetes have reported not following their treatment plan due to cost.
notes.claim: Budget 2024 gives the need figure for diabetes specifically: one in four Canadians with diabetes reported not following their treatment plan because of cost — the cost-related non-adherence the program is meant to address.

notes.quote: The BC PharmaCare National Pharmacare plan (Plan NP) launched on March 1, 2026.
notes.claim: BC's own administrative page (updated 29 June 2026) gives the launch date, the automatic-coverage design and the actual covered list — insulins, metformin, glyburide, gliclazide, dapagliflozin, empagliflozin at 100%, four drugs requiring Special Authority, and six menopausal hormone therapy products. It also shows Plan NP dispenses do not count toward the Fair PharmaCare deductible.

notes.quote: The Province of B.C. and the Government of Canada signed an agreement on March 6, 2025, for federal funding for medication and medical device and supply coverage in B.C., with the federal government providing up to $670 million in funding over three years.
notes.claim: A direct contradiction between governments: BC's page says the federal government provides "up to $670 million in funding over three years," while Health Canada's agreement schedule spreads payments across four fiscal years (2025-26 to 2028-29).

notes.quote: Coverage is automatic at the pharmacy. You do not need to register or submit receipts.
notes.claim: BC confirms coverage is automatic with no registration, and that the federal money supports a provincially administered plan — reinforcing that no federal enrolment count exists.

notes.quote: Effective April 15, 2025, the Manitoba Enhanced Pharmacare Program (MEPP) provides eligible Manitoba residents with no cost coverage of most medications for:
notes.claim: Manitoba's program extends beyond the two federal categories to cover HIV prevention and treatment and hormone replacement therapy at no cost, with federal funding supporting only the diabetes and birth-control portions — provinces are adding benefits on top.

notes.quote: Manitobans who already have 100 per cent coverage through federal or other provincial program such as Indigenous Services Canada’s Non-Insured Health Benefit Program (NIHB) or Manitoba’s Employment Income Assistance Program (EIA) are not eligible for MEPP and should continue to access their medications through these programs.
notes.claim: Manitoba excludes federal-program clients entirely: people with coverage through NIHB or Employment and Income Assistance are not eligible for MEPP and must keep using those programs — so "universal" coverage is layered, not uniform.

notes.quote: Ozempic was not included in the federal list of medications for no-cost coverage for discussion with provinces and territories.
notes.claim: Ozempic (semaglutide) is not covered at no cost in Manitoba because it was not on the federal list for negotiation — concrete evidence that the federal product list, not clinical need, determines what is free.

notes.quote: Diabetes supplies remain as benefits under the Manitoba Pharmacare Program (where deductibles apply), and other provincial programs such as Employment and Income Assistance.
notes.claim: Diabetes supplies remain outside the no-cost program in Manitoba and stay subject to Pharmacare deductibles — the device/supply gap is real at the provincial level despite the separate federal Stream 2 fund.

notes.quote: No. Manitoba Pharmacare Program deductibles do not apply to coverage under MEPP.
notes.claim: Manitoba explicitly states the federal Pharmacare deductibles do not apply to the new program, confirming first-dollar coverage in practice: the provincial income-based deductible is bypassed for covered products.

notes.claim: Health Canada's national pharmacare landing page (dated 2026-01-29) has five sections — about, who is covered, how to access, what products are covered, bilateral agreements — and no section on utilisation, claims, enrolment counts or results; the federal reporting architecture has no place where usage would be published.

notes.claim: Manitoba's own FAQ confirms the four-signatory position from a provincial source: Manitoba signed Canada's first bilateral agreement on 27 February 2025, and the federal initiative funds only diabetes medications and birth control as a "first phase."

notes.claim: BC's Plan NP page was last updated 29 June 2026, and at that date it still described the federal program as covering four jurisdictions — a second government source five months after Health Canada's January 2026 page.
