report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. What the Pharmacare Act actually set up: coverage, funding, and the conditions provinces must meet

The Pharmacare Act (Bill C-64, *An Act respecting pharmacare*) received royal assent on 10 October 2024. What it did not do is create a national pharmacare program. Its operative coverage commitment is conditional and bilateral: federal money flows to a province or territory only if that government signs an agreement with the federal Minister of Health, and the money is earmarked for a defined set of products — prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes.

That conditionality is written into the payment provision itself. Section 6(1) reads: "6 (1) The Minister must, if the Minister has entered into an agreement with a province or territory to do so, make payments to the province or territory in order to increase any existing public pharmacare coverage — and to provide universal, single-payer, first-dollar coverage — for specific prescription drugs and related products intended for contraception or the treatment of diabetes." [4] The obligation on the Minister is triggered by the existence of an agreement, not by residence in Canada. A Canadian living in a province that has not signed has no entitlement under the Act.

The Act also fixes the *terms* of coverage in a way that matters for patients, and it is the one place where the statute is strict. Section 6(2): "For greater certainty, any agreement referred to in subsection (1) with a province or territory is to provide for first-dollar coverage to patients." [4] First-dollar coverage means no deductible and no co-payment at the pharmacy counter for the covered products — the federal contribution is not a subsidy layered on top of an existing provincial deductible scheme but a requirement that the covered items cost the patient nothing. This is the statutory hook for every later federal claim that the covered contraceptives and diabetes drugs are "free."

The purpose clause is deliberately weaker than the payment clause. Section 3 states that the Act's purpose "is to guide efforts to improve, for all Canadians, the accessibility and affordability of prescription drugs and related products, and to support their appropriate use, in collaboration with the provinces, territories, Indigenous peoples and other partners and stakeholders, with the aim of continuing to work toward the implementation of national universal pharmacare." [4] The operative phrase is "continuing to work toward." The Act commits the federal government to a direction of travel, not to a delivered universal program. Section 4 then lists the principles the Minister "is to consider" when collaborating — consistent coverage, affordability, appropriate use and universal coverage — alongside the Canada Health Act. [4] Those are considerations the Minister must weigh, not conditions a province can be audited against or enforced in court. The difference between section 4 ("is to consider") and section 6(2) ("is to provide for") is the difference between aspiration and obligation in this statute, and it explains most of what has and has not happened since.

The Act does carry two non-coverage mandates that run on a longer timeline: a national formulary — a list of prescription drugs to be covered — and a national bulk purchasing strategy. Both were assigned to what was then CADTH, revamped in May 2024 into Canada's Drug Agency. Neither is a coverage commitment, and neither delivers a drug to a patient. They are the machinery that a future comprehensive program would need, and their existence is why the government can describe the current phase as a first step rather than the program itself.

**What "contraception and diabetes" means in practice was decided outside the statute.** The Act names two therapeutic categories but does not list the products. Those lists were published as announcements and backgrounders in February 2024, framed as positions to be negotiated with provinces rather than as schedules to the Act. Health Canada's contraception backgrounder described the intended basket as including "oral contraceptives, copper and hormonal IUDs, injections, implants, rings, and morning-after pills" — a list put forward for discussion with provinces and territories, so that the effective scope of coverage in any given province is fixed by the bilateral agreement, not by the Act. [6]

Diabetes coverage was split in two, and only one half is in the bill. The diabetes medications list was attached to a backgrounder for negotiation, while devices and supplies were handled separately: "Separate from Bill C-64, the federal government is announcing its intention to establish a fund to support access to diabetes devices and supplies. Further details regarding this fund will be provided following discussions with PT partners, who will be essential partners to its roll out." [5] The device fund was thus an intention announced alongside the legislation, not an entitlement created by it, and its details were left to negotiations that had not yet happened when the bill passed. Anyone asking what the Act "covers" is therefore asking a question the Act answers only by reference to documents it does not contain.

Three structural consequences follow, and they organise everything in the rest of this report.

First, coverage is a map of signatures, not of citizenship. The set of people who can walk into a pharmacy and receive a contraceptive or diabetes drug at no charge under this program is exactly the set of people resident in jurisdictions whose governments have signed. The federal role is to transfer money and to set the terms — first-dollar coverage, the two therapeutic categories, reporting obligations — while the provincial or territorial public plan administers and pays. This is the same architecture as the Canada Health Transfer and the dental care plan: federal money, provincial delivery, bilateral agreements as the instrument.

Second, because the program is administered through existing provincial plans, there is no federal enrolment. A resident of a signing province is covered by virtue of holding a provincial health card; there is no registration form, no federal card, no application. That design choice is efficient and it is also why the question "how many people are using it" is so hard to answer — the federal government does not, in the ordinary sense, have a membership list to count.

Third, the fiscal envelope for this phase is small relative to the program the Act gestures at. The first phase was budgeted at $1.5 billion over several years, against full-program estimates in the tens of billions annually. The gap between those numbers is the gap between a proof of concept and a national program, and it is where the cost estimates in the later sections of this report become politically decisive rather than technical.

### 2. Which provinces and territories have signed agreements, when, for how much, and who has not

Four jurisdictions have signed. All four signed within a five-week window in early 2025, and Health Canada's bilateral agreements page — updated 26 January 2026 — still described the count as four: "The Government of Canada has signed funding agreements with four provinces and territories to make a range of contraception and diabetes medications free." [12] That leaves nine provinces and two territories without an agreement roughly eighteen months after royal assent, including Ontario, Quebec, Alberta, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Saskatchewan and the two northern territories other than Yukon. Ontario and Alberta alone account for more than half the Canadian population.

The four, in signing order:

**Manitoba — 27 February 2025.** The first agreement, announced as "this first-ever national pharmacare agreement," with "more than $219 million over four years." [14] The agreement's own schedule sets Stream 1 transfers of $52,509,230 in 2025-26 and $54,603,615 in each of the following three years, plus a one-time $9,945,348 in Stream 2 device funding in 2025-26 [8] — the schedule behind the "more than $219 million" headline [14]. Manitoba's implementation date in the agreement text was 15 April 2025, although the signing release told residents to expect coverage "for the majority of these products in June 2025." [14] Manitoba was therefore the first jurisdiction where the benefit actually existed at a pharmacy counter.

**British Columbia — 6 March 2025.** The largest agreement: "more than $670 million over four years," covering contraceptives, diabetes medications, devices and supplies. [13] Stream 1 payments are $17,406,567 in 2025-26, then $204,948,289 in each of 2026-27, 2027-28 and 2028-29; a one-time Stream 2 payment of $37,839,549 arrives in 2026-27 [7]. That schedule is the basis of the "more than $670 million" in the signing release [13]. The fiscal profile is unusual and revealing: BC's first-year transfer is $17,406,567 against $204,948,289 in each later year, about a twelfth, because its implementation date was set for 1 March 2026. [7] BC signed in March 2025 and went live in March 2026. As a condition of the deal, BC also agreed to add free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms from 1 March 2026, a benefit outside the Act's two categories and funded by the province. [13]

**Prince Edward Island — 7 March 2025.** "More than $30 million over four years." [15] The schedule gives $6,795,833 in 2025-26 and $7,404,416 in each of the next three years, plus $1,188,243 one-time for devices [10] — the "more than $30 million" headline [15]. PEI's implementation date was 1 May 2025, making it the second jurisdiction live. [10]

**Yukon — 20 March 2025.** "Up to $9.5 million over four years." [16] Stream 1 transfers are $2,548,410 in 2026-27 and $2,650,056 in each of 2027-28 and 2028-29, plus $306,143 one-time for devices [9] — a schedule that begins only in 2026-27 and sits below the "up to $9.5 million" headline [16]. Yukon's implementation date in the agreement is "between April 15 and May 5, 2026" [9], which contradicts the signing release's promise that "Yukon residents can anticipate beginning to receive coverage for these products no later than January 2026." [16] On the agreement's own text, Yukoners were covered more than a year after their government signed, and three to four months later than the federal announcement said.

**The pattern in the dates is the finding.** Signing an agreement and delivering a benefit are separate events, separated by between one and fourteen months. Manitoba signed and implemented in about seven weeks. PEI took about eight weeks. BC took almost exactly twelve months. Yukon took at least thirteen. The federal money is committed at signing, but the pharmacy counter changes only at the implementation date, which each province sets in its own agreement.

Two further observations from the numbers. First, the allocation is not proportional to need but to population and to existing provincial spending baselines: BC's $670 million is roughly three times Manitoba's $226 million, which is roughly seven times PEI's $30 million, which is roughly three and a half times Yukon's $8.2 million. Second, the published headline figures do not add up to the first-phase envelope usually described as $1.5 billion: more than $670 million for BC [13], more than $219 million for Manitoba [14], more than $30 million for PEI [15] and up to $9.5 million for Yukon [16] leave a large remainder unallocated. Either the rest is being held for agreements not yet signed, or the headline envelope covers spending not captured in these four schedules. This report could not reconcile the two from published sources, and the gap is worth stating rather than smoothing over.

Nothing in the record shows an agreement with any of the holdouts. Alberta's government had publicly opposed a national pharmacare program in principle before the Act passed, arguing for an opt-out with compensation; Ontario and Quebec did not sign in the first eighteen months despite being the two largest provincial drug plans in the country. Whether the absence of agreements reflects negotiation, opposition or simple sequencing is not documented in the sources this report could read, and should be treated as an open question rather than as evidence of refusal.

### 3. What is covered in practice: drug lists, devices, deductibles, and what patients still pay

What a patient gets is narrower than "free birth control and diabetes drugs," and the qualifications are documented on the government's own pages rather than in commentary.

**The basket is a negotiated list, not a category.** Coverage runs to "a range of birth control options and diabetes medications" and applies to the products listed in each agreement's Annex A. [21] The Act names two therapeutic areas; the annexes name the drugs. That means the basket can differ between jurisdictions and can be extended by negotiation — which is exactly what BC did, adding free public coverage of hormone replacement therapy for menopausal symptoms from 1 March 2026 as part of its deal, a benefit outside the Act's two categories and funded by the province rather than the federal transfer. [13]

**First-dollar coverage applies to the drug and the dispensing fee — not to everything at the counter.** Health Canada's page is precise: pharmacare "only covers the costs of listed products and medications, including the dispensing fee" and it will not cover delivery fees or pharmacist prescribing fees. [21] The bilateral agreements page adds the same caveat in softer language, saying products "will be available for free or at low cost at the pharmacy counter" and that "Other fees, such as prescribing fees or delivery fees, may still apply." [12] Two consequences follow. First, in provinces where a pharmacist must prescribe the contraceptive — increasingly common for hormonal contraception — the patient can still pay a prescribing fee for a drug that is nominally free. Second, the statutory "first-dollar coverage" guarantee in section 6(2) of the Act [4] covers the drug; it does not reach the professional fees around it, so the "no cost to patients" claim is true of the product and not of the transaction.

**There is no deductible and no co-payment on the covered products, and private insurance is bypassed rather than coordinated.** The bilateral agreements page tells patients: "You **won't** need to coordinate benefits with private insurance plans." [12] This is a design choice with real effects: a person with employer drug coverage does not submit the pharmacare claim to the private plan first, and the public plan does not act as a second payer. The covered product is paid at first dollar by the public plan, and the private plan's role in that product ends. For someone with a workplace plan and a deductible, this is a straightforward gain. For the private plan, it is a transfer of liability to the public system — which is where the "fill-the-gaps" critique in section 6 comes from, and why the PBO's model treats the program as topping up rather than replacing.

**Additionality is enforced, not assumed.** The agreements require each province to report what it spent in 2022-23 on exactly the products in Annex A, and they let Canada claw back money if that baseline was overstated. The PEI agreement's clause is explicit: where the province's reported 2022-23 Stream 1 spending is greater than the amount reported elsewhere in the agreement, the agreement provides that "Canada will withhold or reduce an amount equivalent to the difference between these two amounts" [10]. The purpose is to stop a province from substituting federal money for its own spending and calling it new coverage. Manitoba's Annex B shows how the test bites: Manitoba spent $23,195,236 on the diabetes products in the list and $750,746 on the contraceptives in 2022-23, for a total of $23,945,982 [8] — against a first-year federal transfer of $52,509,230 [8]. Federal money therefore more than doubles the provincial baseline for these products, which is the concrete meaning of "increase any existing public pharmacare coverage" in section 6(1) of the Act [4].

**What the benefit is worth to a patient is substantial and unevenly distributed.** Health Canada puts metformin at "about $100 per year," insulin at "between $900 and $1,700 per year," and sulfonylureas and SGLT-2 inhibitors at "from $100 to over $1,000 per year." [2] For people with the highest costs, the federal announcement cites Diabetes Canada's 2022 finding that out-of-pocket costs ran "as high as $18,306 per year for people living with Type 1 diabetes and as high as $10,014 per year for those living with Type 2 diabetes." [13] Those figures are the upper tail — they include devices, supplies and monitoring, not just the listed drugs — but they explain why the benefit is politically salient out of proportion to its fiscal size. A program of a few hundred million dollars a year can remove a cost of the size Diabetes Canada measured from a household with Type 1 diabetes, and that is the kind of change voters notice.

**The need the program addresses is broad and was measured before it existed.** The BC announcement cites Statistics Canada's 2021 finding that "one in five adults in Canada did not have the insurance they needed to cover their medication costs." [13] That is the baseline against which the program should be judged, and it is a national figure for a program that in its first eighteen months reached four jurisdictions. In PEI, the federal announcement made the local case directly: "Here in Prince Edward Island, residents face some of Canada's highest out-of-pocket costs for drugs covered on their public plans." [15] The provinces that signed first were not the ones with the weakest coverage on average; they were the ones whose governments chose to sign.

**What is not covered matters as much as what is.** Diabetes devices and supplies sit in a separate Stream 2 fund announced outside the Act, not in the section 6 entitlement [5], and the amounts are small relative to the drug transfers — $37,839,549 for BC in 2026-27 [7], $9,945,348 for Manitoba [8], $1,188,243 for PEI [10], $306,143 for Yukon [9]. Everything else — every cancer drug, every biologic for inflammatory disease, every antibiotic, every cardiovascular medicine, and the whole of the expensive specialty segment that drives most drug spending growth — remains outside this program entirely. The Act's first phase covers two therapeutic areas out of the dozens that matter to patients, and the report of the Committee of Experts published in 2025 was blunt that this architecture is not the one it recommended (see section 6).

### 4. How many people are actually using it: enrolment, claims, and what is counted

This is the weakest-evidenced part of the pharmacare story, and the weakness is structural rather than a failure of reporting. The design of the program makes "how many people are using it" a question that no federal dataset answers directly.

The reason is that there is no federal enrolment. Coverage in a signing jurisdiction is automatic for anyone eligible for that province's or territory's health insurance. Health Canada's own page for the public is explicit that the program does not screen anyone out on the criteria that usually gate a benefit: "You're covered under pharmacare no matter your: age income private or workplace health insurance status" [3] A resident of British Columbia, Manitoba, Prince Edward Island or Yukon who holds a health card is covered by operation of the bilateral agreement and the provincial plan, not by any act of registration. The federal government therefore has no membership roll to publish, and the number "covered" in those four jurisdictions is a population figure — an estimate of eligible residents — rather than a count of people who have signed up or used the benefit.

This matters because the two numbers that get conflated in public discussion are very different quantities. The number *eligible* in the four signed jurisdictions is in the range of several million people, since it is essentially the combined population of BC, Manitoba, PEI and Yukon, narrowed only by the requirement to hold provincial health insurance. The number *actually dispensing a covered contraceptive or diabetes drug at zero cost* is smaller and is a claims statistic, held by provincial drug plans and by pharmacies, not by Health Canada.

The scale of the eligible clinical population is itself an estimate. Health Canada's pharmacare pages give the diabetes figure directly: "About 3.8 million people in Canada have been diagnosed with diabetes. In 2018, costs to the healthcare system related to diabetes were estimated at $27 billion, and they could surpass $39 billion by 2028." [2] That 3.8 million is the national denominator. It is not the pharmacare-eligible population — only the share of those people living in the four signing jurisdictions is eligible — but it sets the outer bound, and it shows how modest the current footprint is: at most a fraction of 3.8 million people with diabetes, plus the larger population of people using contraception, most of whom are not counted in any diabetes statistic.

The contraception denominator is harder still, because the eligible group is defined by need for a product rather than by a diagnosis. There is no equivalent of a diabetes registry. A provincial plan knows how many contraceptive prescriptions it filled at zero cost; it does not know how many people would have filled one if the product were free, which is the counterfactual that a take-up rate requires.

Health Canada's own summary of progress, on a page updated in January 2026, described the state of play as four agreements: "We've signed funding agreements with 4 provinces and territories to make a range of contraception (birth control) and diabetes medications free at the pharmacy counter." [2] That sentence is the federal government's own account of what has been delivered at the point of coverage — and it is a statement about agreements signed, not about prescriptions filled or patients served. The department's public reporting on the program is built around the signing of agreements, the products covered and the absence of cost to patients; it is not built around utilisation counts.

What would be needed to answer the usage question properly is provincial dispensing data for the covered products, before and after the agreement came into force, with a breakdown by drug class and by whether the recipient had prior public or private coverage. Some provinces publish drug plan utilization statistics; whether any of them have published a pharmacare-specific series is a separate question, and one this report has not been able to settle from federal sources. Until those series exist and are comparable across jurisdictions, any national figure for "people using pharmacare" is an inference from population and prescribing patterns, not a measurement — and should be labelled as such wherever it appears.

### 5. What the Parliamentary Budget Officer says the full program would cost, and on what assumptions

The Parliamentary Budget Officer has published three costings that bear on this question, and they answer three different questions. Confusing them is the single most common error in public discussion of pharmacare costs.

**1. The current phase: $1.9 billion over five years.** The PBO's legislative costing note on Bill C-64 found "the first phase of national universal pharmacare will increase federal program spending by $1.9 billion over five years," on the explicit assumption "that any medications that are currently covered by provincial and territorial governments, as well as private insurance providers will remain covered on the same terms." [11] The PBO's framing of the program's purpose is equally important: "The aim of the program is to expand and enhance, rather than replace, existing provincial and territorial coverage." [20]

The method is worth setting out because it determines what the number means. The model assumes the program "will cover 100% of the expense on diabetes and contraception medication for those who currently do not have public or private drug plan coverage and for those who currently do not fill their prescriptions due to cost related reasons," with the latter group "assumed to be 14% of total prescriptions," and that it will also cover "the out-of-pocket portion of prescription costs for those who have public or private drug plan coverage." [20] In other words: for the uninsured, the program pays the whole cost; for the insured, it pays only the deductible and co-payment. That is why $1.9 billion over five years is small — it is the cost of the gaps, not the cost of the drugs.

The PBO was candid about the limits. "The estimate has high uncertainty and is contingent on the number of drugs listed for coverage." [20] The model assumes no new federal confidential rebates, because the program's objective is to expand rather than replace existing plans — but notes that if the administrator negotiates rebates, "it will reduce the cost of the program." It excludes substitution from unlisted drugs to listed ones, which would raise cost, and it excludes savings to the Medical Expense Tax Credit. Drug expenditure and mark-up data came from IQVIA for 2021-22, projected using Patented Medicine Prices Review Board growth rates; copper IUD costs were estimated from 2017 General Social Survey prevalence data adjusted by average IUD duration. [20]

**2. The full program on a comprehensive list: $35 billion gross, $11.9 billion incremental.** The PBO's 2023 report costed public funding of a national pharmacare program using Quebec's RAMQ formulary as the drug list. As the Committee of Experts summarized it: "The estimated total cost of publicly funding a longer list of medicines (the RAMQ list from Quebec) was $35 billion in 2025 to 26. The incremental cost to the public sector $11.9 billion. For a shorter list of essential medicines, the estimated cost in 2025 to 26 was $9.8 billion." [17]

The distinction between $35 billion and $11.9 billion is the whole analytical crux. The $35 billion is the gross public bill for covering the list — money that would flow through the public plan for drugs now paid for by private plans, out of pocket, or already by provinces. The $11.9 billion is the *incremental* public cost after accounting for existing public spending being reallocated to the new program. Quoting $35 billion as "the cost of pharmacare" without saying it is gross, and that $23 billion of it is a transfer rather than new spending, is a category error — but so is quoting $11.9 billion without saying that it assumes existing provincial spending is folded in.

**3. The full program on an essential medicines list: $9.8 billion.** The same 2023 report costed a shorter essential medicines list at $9.8 billion for 2025-26. This is the number the Committee of Experts adopted as its upper bound. [17]

The PBO's modelling choice on utilization is where its estimates are most contestable, and the Committee of Experts contested it. "Some studies have found no increases in use with public coverage, while others have found increases above 10%. We selected 5% for our lower bound estimate, while the upper bound estimate from the Parliamentary Budget Office assumes an increase of 13.5%, which is larger than estimates in the literature." [17] A 13.5% assumption for the increase in medicine use once coverage is free is at the top of the empirical range; the Committee treated that conservatism as a reason its own lower figure was defensible, not as a reason the PBO was wrong.

**What the numbers mean together.** Total Canadian spending on prescribed drugs "jumped by $10 billion in 5 years – from $34 billion in 2019 to $44 billion in 2024." [17] Set against that $44 billion base, the full-program estimates are: $9.8 billion on an essential list (about 22% of current total spending, gross), $11.9 billion incremental on a comprehensive list, and $35 billion gross on a comprehensive list. The phase now being delivered is $1.9 billion over five years — roughly $380 million a year, or under 1% of current prescription drug spending. The enacted program is smaller than every full-program estimate by at least one order of magnitude, and smaller than the gross comprehensive estimate by nearly two.

**The gap between the PBO's $1.9 billion and the money actually committed.** Budget 2024 is the source of the first-phase envelope: "Budget 2024 proposes to provide $1.5 billion over five years, starting in 2024-25, to Health Canada to support the launch of the National Pharmacare Plan." [23] That $1.5 billion sits above the PBO's $1.9 billion? No — below it. The PBO's own costing of the identical phase is the larger number, which is unusual: a central agency's legislative costing normally comes in under the budgeted envelope, not above it.

Against those two figures sit the four signed agreements: more than $670 million for BC [13], more than $219 million for Manitoba [14], more than $30 million for PEI [15] and up to $9.5 million for Yukon [16]. Added together these fall well short of both the $1.5 billion budgeted and the $1.9 billion costed.

Three differences could explain the shortfall, and it is important to say which parts are documented and which are this report's inference. Documented: the PBO's five-year window starts in 2024-25, while the agreements' payment schedules begin in 2025-26 (Manitoba, PEI) or 2026-27 (Yukon), and BC's schedule front-loads only $17,406,567 in 2025-26 before rising to $204,948,289 a year [7][8][9][10]. Documented: BC's own page describes the federal contribution as "up to $670 million in funding over three years" [24], whereas Health Canada's schedule spreads payments across four fiscal years [7] — the two governments do not describe the same agreement the same way. Inference, and labelled as such: the remainder of the envelope is most plausibly unallocated money held for agreements not yet signed, since nine provinces and two territories have none, and neither Health Canada nor the PBO has published a reconciliation tying the budgeted envelope, the legislative costing and the signed schedules together.

**Where the PBO's estimate is strongest and weakest.** Strongest: the $1.9 billion figure, because it is a legislative costing with published method, IQVIA data and explicit behavioural assumptions, and because the first year of actual transfers can be checked against it. Weakest: the full-program estimates, because they rest on a formulary that does not exist — the national formulary the Act mandated is a list, not a negotiated set of prices — and on rebate assumptions that the PBO explicitly set at zero for the phase-one costing and could not observe for the comprehensive ones. The $11.9 billion incremental figure in particular depends on how much existing provincial spending is counted as reallocated rather than additive, and that accounting has not been done publicly for any province.

### 6. Other independent estimates — the Advisory Council, academics, think tanks — and why they diverge from the PBO

The PBO is not the only body to have costed national pharmacare, and the estimates differ by a factor of two or more. Understanding why is more useful than picking a number, because the differences are almost entirely about what is being costed — a defined basket of essential medicines, or a comprehensive formulary covering everything a province currently lists and more.

**The Advisory Council on the Implementation of National Pharmacare** — chaired by Dr. Eric Hoskins, reporting in June 2019 — remains the most detailed public model, and it is the source of most of the numbers in circulation. Its headline: "We have estimated that it will cost an additional $3.5 billion in 2022 to launch national pharmacare starting with universal coverage for essential medicines." [1] That $3.5 billion figure is a *first-step* number, covering a limited list of essential medicines, and it is routinely misquoted as the cost of pharmacare. The Council's own projection for a comprehensive program is much larger: additional public spending rising to $15.3 billion a year by 2027 as the formulary phases in and becomes comprehensive.

The Council was careful to reconcile its work with the PBO's earlier costing, and that reconciliation is the most valuable passage in the report for anyone comparing estimates. The PBO had found that "if national pharmacare had been fully implemented in 2015-16, it would have required incremental public spending of $7.3 billion ($6.3 billion net of copayment revenues and ancillary savings). Overall, this would amount to a 50-55 per cent increase in public spending on prescription drugs." [1] So: PBO at $7.3 billion gross for a 2015-16 implementation, against a Council figure of $15.3 billion for 2027. Neither is wrong. They are costing different years, different formularies and different baselines.

The Council warns against comparing the two numbers directly: "It is difficult, however, to directly compare the results of the council’s drug spending model with those of the PBO. While the council’s model builds on the methodology used by the PBO, it is not identical and uses assumptions about the key drivers of prescription drug spending to project future drug costs." [1] The Council's point is that its model projects future drug costs rather than costing a program in a single year.

What separates the two figures is then a matter of what each model contains, and here the sources are explicit on two of the three differences. Time is the first: the PBO costed implementation in 2015-16 and the Council projects to 2027, so the later number absorbs more than a decade of inflation, population growth, population aging and the arrival of expensive new drugs. Scope is the second, and it is stated plainly — the PBO's $7.3 billion was for "national pharmacare... fully implemented," while the Council's $3.5 billion launch figure covers only "universal coverage for essential medicines," with the $15.3 billion arriving only "as the formulary becomes comprehensive." [1] The third difference — that the Council's figure is an increment over a provincial system assumed to keep growing — follows from the Council's own framing of its model as projecting "future drug costs" [1], and is this report's reading rather than a sentence in the report.

The practical consequence is that "$15.3 billion" and "$7.3 billion" are not competing estimates of the same thing, and citing either as "the cost of pharmacare" without the year, the formulary and the baseline misstates what was measured.

On one point the two estimates converge, and it is the point that matters most for the fiscal argument: both find that a single-payer bulk-purchasing model would produce system-wide savings that offset a meaningful share of the gross cost. The PBO's $7.3 billion gross becomes $6.3 billion net of "copayment revenues and ancillary savings" [1] — a reduction of about 14 per cent. The Council's model finds larger potential savings from formulary consolidation and bulk purchasing, because a comprehensive single payer can drive harder bargains than a patchwork of provincial plans. This is the analytic basis for the claim, made by pharmacare advocates across the political spectrum, that universal single-payer coverage is not simply a new expenditure but a partial substitution for spending that already happens through private plans, out-of-pocket payments and higher provincial drug prices.

The estimates that matter for the current phase are of a different order of magnitude entirely. The first phase — contraception and diabetes drugs and devices, delivered through bilateral agreements — was budgeted at $1.5 billion. Against the Council's $15.3 billion a year for a comprehensive program, that is roughly a tenth of one year's full cost, spread over several years. The arithmetic is the clearest statement available of how far the 2024 Act is from the program the 2019 report described: the enacted program is a single-digit percentage of the modelled one.

**Where the numbers are weakest.** Both the PBO and Council models rest on assumptions that have not been tested against delivery. Neither could anticipate the actual pattern of provincial signing, which determines the real federal outlay in the current phase. Neither models the counterfactual that matters most for evaluating phase one: how much of the $1.5 billion substitutes for spending that would have happened anyway — through provincial plans, employer plans or out-of-pocket payments — rather than adding new coverage. If a province already covered diabetes drugs for low-income residents and the federal agreement extends that to everyone, the increment is the newly covered population, not the whole cost of the prescriptions. None of the published estimates isolate that increment, and until a provincial audit does, the true cost per newly covered person in phase one is unknown.

There is also a political-economy gap in the literature. The models cost a program delivered uniformly across ten provinces and three territories. The delivered program is a sequence of bilateral deals at different times, with different terms, in jurisdictions of wildly different size. The fiscal consequence is that federal spending in this phase is driven by which governments sign, not by which residents need coverage — a feature the PBO's national models are not built to capture and which no independent body has yet costed.
