q: What does the evidence say about school smartphone bans: which jurisdictions (Ontario, England, the Netherlands, Australian states and others) have adopted them, what have evaluations measured about learning, attention, bullying and mental health, and how strong is that evidence?

report.title: School smartphone bans: which jurisdictions have adopted them, what evaluations measure, and how strong the evidence is

groups.sample: a 2 phone ban yes no 2 time baseline follow up repeated measures design chosen to align with the department

notes.quote: The empirical work in this paper finds no clear evidence of beneficial mental health effectsfrom state mandated school bans on smartphones.
notes.claim: US NBER working paper (Saffer, 2026), synthetic difference-in-differences on National Survey of Children's Health 2016-2024, finds no clear evidence of beneficial mental health effects from state school smartphone bans.

notes.quote: Post-ban bullying among both genders also decreased.
notes.claim: Norway study (Abrahamsson, Journal of Human Resources): school-level staggered smartphone bans improved girls' mental health significantly; post-ban bullying fell among both genders.

notes.quote: All schools should be mobile phone-free environments by default; anything other than this should be by exception only.
notes.claim: England's DfE guidance requires schools to prohibit mobile phone use throughout the school day — lessons, between lessons, breaktimes and lunchtime — with exceptions only. First published 19 February 2024; revised January 2026 and became statutory on 29 June 2026, with schools to follow from 1 September 2026.

notes.quote:
Students Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobiles devices during class time without the explicit permission of their teacher.

Students Grade 6 and below may not use cellphones or other mobile devices at school during the school day without the permission of a teacher.
notes.claim: Ontario's rules: students Grade 7 and above may not use cellphones or other mobile devices during class time without explicit teacher permission; students Grade 6 and below may not use them at school during the school day without teacher permission. The updated provincial Code of Conduct took effect September 1, 2024, and boards must have an enforcement policy and remind parents annually.

notes.quote: No short-term changes emerged in social loneliness, friend support, or cyberbullying victimization, although cyberbullying perpetration declined slightly. Over time, social loneliness increased modestly, friend support remained stable, and cyberbullying fluctuated at low levels.
notes.claim: Flanders (Belgium) study, 960 secondary students followed across 8 waves over one school year around a total smartphone ban: no short-term change in social loneliness, friend support or cyberbullying victimisation, only a slight decline in perpetration; loneliness rose modestly over the year.

notes.quote: Results indicated no significant differences between ban and no-ban schools in school belonging, academic engagement or problematic phone use, but bullying declined significantly in both groups over time.
notes.claim: King et al. (2024) natural experiment in two groups of schools found no significant difference between ban and no-ban schools in school belonging, academic engagement or problematic phone use, and bullying declined significantly in both groups over time.

notes.quote: The only study to date to investigate smartphone bans in schools in relation to students’ screentime and problematic social media use, indicates that students’ screentime after school increases to compensate for restrictions during school hours, and found no differences for problematic usage (Goodyear et al., 2025).
notes.claim: Displacement: a UK study found students' screen time rose after school, compensating for in-school restrictions — evidence that bans may displace rather than reduce phone use.

notes.quote: Currently, there is only one study comparing the effectiveness of these various types of smartphone bans in the UK (Goodyear et al., 2025), finding no differences between different types of bans for several different outcomes of mental health, physical activity, disruptive classroom behaviour and problematic social media use.
notes.claim: The UK comparison of partial vs full bans found no differences in disruptive classroom behaviour — directly relevant to the attention/engagement question.

notes.quote: In this study, we try to fill this gap by examining the causal effects of bans on student test scores, suspensions, and absences using detailed student-level data from Florida and a quasi-experimental research strategy relying upon differences in pre-ban cellphone use by students, as measured by building-level Advan data.
notes.claim: The main US causal study (Figlio & Özek, NBER WP 34388, Oct 2025) is quasi-experimental, not a randomised trial: it exploits variation in pre-ban building-level phone activity to compare more- and less-affected schools in one large Florida district.

notes.quote: There were no statistically significant changes in test scores during the first year of the ban, when disciplinary rates were high. During the second year of the ban, in contrast, test scores increased significantly, with positive effects concentrated during the spring semester (scores increased 1.1 percentiles, on average).
notes.claim: Even in the strongest US study the measured effect is small and delayed: no significant score change in year one, about 1.1 percentile points in year two, with suspensions up 25% initially — a reminder that effect sizes and timing are sensitive to the outcome window chosen.

notes.quote: Empirical findings for well-being outcomes are also scarce and mixed: Two studies found no significant effects of smartphone bans at school on students’ well-being (Guldvik & Kvinnsland, 2018; Goodyear et al., 2025), while another reported reduced mental health care needs for girls only (Abrahamsson, 2024).
notes.claim: Dutch study reports that prior evidence on well-being is scarce and mixed: two studies found no significant effects on wellbeing, one found reduced mental health care needs for girls only; and two older studies found cyberbullying was more frequent in schools with restrictions.

notes.quote: No significant differences were found for any of the well-being or bullying outcomes. However, full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging.
notes.claim: Dutch EPoSS study (2024-25, 1,398 students, 24 schools): no significant differences between full and partial bans on any well-being or bullying outcome; full bans associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, lower school belonging.

notes.quote:
**Date of Issue:** June 27, 2024

**Effective:** September 1, 2024
notes.claim: Ontario PPM 128 was issued 27 June 2024 and effective 1 September 2024, replacing the 2019 memorandum. It sets the Provincial Code of Conduct requirement that no member of the school community use personal mobile devices during instructional time except for educational purposes as directed by an educator, for health/medical purposes, or to support special education needs.

notes.quote: School boards are required to restrict access to all social media platforms on school networks and school devices.
notes.claim: Ontario's PPM 128 requires boards to restrict all social media platforms on school networks and school devices, and mandates that report cards beginning 2024-25 communicate information about classroom distractions including those related to personal mobile device use.

notes.quote: No significant differences in mental health outcomes were found between ban versus no-ban groups based on social media posting levels.
notes.claim: South Australia (Radunz et al., 2025/26, 5 schools, 1,319 students baseline, 603 at follow-up around the Term 3 2023 ban): no significant differences in mental health outcomes between ban and no-ban groups by social media posting level; but higher posting frequency associated with greater psychological distress and self-harm thoughts/behaviours.

notes.quote: Kessel, Hardardottir, and Tyrefors (2020) attempted to replicate Beland and Murphy's study in their study of 1,086 schools in Sweden. In contrast to Beland and Murphy's study, Kessel et al. reported no improvement in student performance in schools with a phone ban.
notes.claim: The Swedish replication on 1,086 schools found no test-score improvement from bans, contradicting Beland & Murphy — a direct disagreement in the attainment literature.

notes.quote: The authors reported an improvement in student academic performance among lower-achieving students following the ban, whereas the high achievers were neither positively nor negatively affected. Beland and Murphy estimated the impact of banning phones for low-achieving students was the equivalent of an additional hour a week in school or five additional school days a year.
notes.claim: Beland & Murphy found UK ban gains concentrated among lower-achieving students, equal to about an extra hour a week or five school days a year; high achievers unaffected.

notes.quote: Using administrative and survey data with an event-study design, I show that banning smartphones in middle schools has no average effect on education or mental health but masks important gender differences. Bans reduce psychological health care use among girls, lower bullying for both genders, and improve girls’ GPAs and academic track placement, especially among those from disadvantaged backgrounds.
notes.claim: Abrahamsson (Norway, event-study, admin data): no average effect of middle-school smartphone bans on education outcomes, but improved girls' GPAs and academic track placement, especially for disadvantaged girls.

notes.quote: In addition, adolescents attending schools with restrictive phone policies did not differ in their sleep duration and efficiency, physical activity, academic attainment, and disruptive classroom behaviour, compared to pupils who attended schools where phone use was permitted during the school day. One potential explanation for this lack of observed difference, is that restrictive school phone policies did not lower the overall time adolescents spent on their phones/social media.
notes.claim: Teacher-rated disruptive classroom behaviour did not differ between restrictive and permissive English schools — i.e., no measured gain in classroom engagement/behaviour from bans in the best UK study.

notes.quote: The median smartphone time in school was 0.38 h (IQR 0.02–1.46) and was greater in permissive schools (1 h, IQR 0.50–2.00) compared to restrictive (0.17 h, IQR 0.00–1.00)
notes.claim: Scale of in-school phone use: median 1 hour per school day in permissive English schools versus 10 minutes in restrictive ones — showing both that phone use during school hours is substantial and that rules do not eliminate it.

notes.quote: Mean WEMWBS score was 47 (SD = 9) with no evidence of a difference between groups (adjusted mean difference −0.48, 95% CI −2.05 to 1.06, p = 0.62).
notes.claim: SMART Schools primary result: no difference in mental wellbeing between restrictive and permissive English schools, with the confidence interval excluding the 3-point minimum clinically important difference.

notes.quote: The UN reported that one in four countries (including France, Israel, and Turkey, as well as regions of Canada and Australia) have introduced laws that mandate public schools to prohibit phone use during the school day.
notes.claim: Scale of adoption: about a quarter of countries had laws mandating phone prohibition in schools by early 2025, per the UN.

notes.quote: No significant differences in pupil outcomes were observed between permissive and restrictive schools for all other behavioural outcomes (Fig. 2, Table 3) or for attainment in English (adjusted odds ratio 1.45, 95% CI 0.85–2.47, p = 0.18, reference = permissive) and Maths (adjusted odds ratio 1.01, 95% CI 0.45–2.27, p = 0.98, reference = permissive).
notes.claim: Attainment measured by teacher reports: no significant difference in English or maths attainment between policy types.

notes.quote: Around 40% of countries in the world (e.g., the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Israel, Turkey, Bangladesh, the United States, and certain areas in Canada and Australia) have enacted laws restricting smartphone use during school hours (UNESCO, 2023).
notes.claim: Adoption scale per UNESCO: around 40% of countries have enacted laws restricting smartphone use during school hours, with named examples including the Netherlands, Belgium, France, Israel, Turkey, Bangladesh, the US, and areas of Canada and Australia.

notes.quote: While there are some studies that report an increase in academic performance after implementation of smartphone bans (e.g., Abrahamsson, 2024), there are almost an equal number of studies that report no differences in academic performance irrespective of bans (e.g., Kessel et al., 2020). It could be argued that there seems to be a negative although small impact of smartphone bans on academic outcomes, but only in certain circumstances for certain students (Campbell et al., 2024).
notes.claim: Review of the attainment literature: about as many studies find gains as find nothing, and the defensible summary is a small negative impact only in certain circumstances for certain students.

notes.quote: The Netherlands introduced a smartphone ban in secondary schools in January 2024
notes.claim: The Netherlands introduced a smartphone ban in secondary schools in January 2024, with school boards left to set their own arrangements, producing partial and full bans.

notes.quote: All government, Catholic and independent schools must restrict student use of personal electronic devices during the school day. This is a requirement of the Education and Training Reform Act 2006 and Ministerial Order No. 1515 – Personal Electronic Devices in Victorian Schools (Ministerial Order 1515).
notes.claim: Victoria requires all government, Catholic and independent schools to restrict student use of personal electronic devices during the school day under the Education and Training Reform Act 2006 and Ministerial Order 1515; from the start of 2027 phones and smart glasses must be switched off and stored with access restricted.

notes.quote:
reduce unnecessary distraction in the classroom
promote more social interaction and physical activity during break times.
notes.claim: Victoria's stated aims for the restriction are reducing health, safety and privacy risks, reducing classroom distraction, and promoting social interaction and physical activity at break.

notes.quote: One-quarter of countries had banned cellphones in schools through a law or policy by 2023, increasing to 31 percent in 2024. In the United States, as of September 2025, 30 states have passed statewide bans or have recommended local districts to enact their own bans or restrictive policies (Prothero, Langreo, and Klein, 2025).
notes.claim: Global adoption counts: one quarter of countries had banned cellphones in schools by law or policy by 2023, rising to 31% in 2024; in the US, 30 states had passed statewide bans or recommended local bans as of September 2025.

notes.quote: LUSD took an even more prohibitive approach to cellphone use in schools. While the statewide ban only requires districts to ban wireless communication devices “during instructional time”, LUSD requires that wireless communications device(s) be silenced and put away in students’ backpacks or purse during the entire school day while on campus, including lunchtime and transitioning between classes.
notes.claim: Florida's HB 379, enacted July 2023, bans wireless devices during instructional time only; the district studied (one of the ten largest in the US) went further, requiring devices silenced and put away for the whole school day including lunch and transitions, with suspension available as a sanction after a grace period ending 4 September 2023.

notes.quote: Relative to the same month in 2022-23, the school year before the cellphone ban, disciplinary incident and suspension rates jumped by roughly 25 percent (increases in disciplinary incident and suspension rates of 43 and 50, respectively, per 10,000 students in the first year of the policy, once it was being fully enforced).
notes.claim: Enforcement, not the rule itself, drove the Florida discipline spike: suspensions rose 25% relative to the same month a year before once the district began referring students for phone infractions, and the effect fell hardest on Black students, with in-school suspensions up about 30% for that group.

notes.quote: In this repeated cross-sectional study of adolescents in Iceland, schoolwide mobile phone bans were not associated with meaningful changes in adolescent mental health or related social and behavioral outcomes.
notes.claim: Iceland's largest test: repeated cross-section of 70 schools, 23,938 adolescent observations across 2016, 2018 and 2023 waves; 22 of 70 schools adopted bans between 2018 and 2023; difference-in-differences found no meaningful change in depressive symptoms, anxiety, hostility or mental wellbeing.

notes.quote: Schools classified as having a phone ban explicitly prohibited student phone use during school hours, with students being required to leave phones at home or store them in lockers or schoolbags. Enforcement typically involved recording infractions in school communication platforms visible to parents, with repeated violations leading to parent meetings.
notes.claim: Icelandic bans are school-level, not national: schools explicitly prohibited phone use during school hours, requiring phones left at home or stored in lockers or bags, with infractions recorded in systems visible to parents and repeated violations leading to parent meetings.

notes.quote: Policymakers have responded by sharply restricting phone use in schools: as of 2026, roughly two-thirds of U.S. states and more than half of countries worldwide have enacted legislation limiting student phone access (D’Addio, 2025; Prothero, Langreo and Klein, 2026).
notes.claim: Scale of adoption as of 2026: roughly two-thirds of US states and more than half of countries worldwide have legislation limiting student phone access; nearly 5,000 US schools use lockable pouches.

notes.quote: The share of students reported to be using their phones in class for personal reasons falls from 61 percent to 13 percent following Yondr adoption (a drop of roughly 80 percent), a substantially larger decline than in non-adopting schools.
notes.claim: The strongest measured effect on phone use in school: teacher-reported share of students using phones in class for personal reasons fell from 61% to 13% after pouch adoption, roughly an 80% drop.

notes.quote: we can rule out improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations
notes.claim: Precision of the null on attainment: the study can rule out test-score improvements larger than about 0.007 student-level standard deviations, i.e. essentially nothing.

notes.quote: The estimate is -0.088 (SE = 0.085), indicating no evidence of changes following adoption.
notes.claim: Classroom attention measured directly: ATT estimate -0.088 (SE 0.085), no evidence of change, with pre-trends limiting interpretation.

notes.quote: The estimate is -0.039 (SE = 0.092), which is small and not statistically significant.
notes.claim: Online bullying in the national pouch study: ATT -0.039 (SE 0.092), small and not statistically significant, with caution due to differential pre-trends in outcome availability.

notes.quote: In the year of implementation, SWB declines sharply by approximately 0.603 school-level standard deviations and then recovers, becoming positive and statistically significant by t + 2 (approximately 0.485 standard deviations).
notes.claim: Wellbeing in the national pouch study falls sharply in the year of adoption and then recovers and turns positive: pooled ATT -0.305, year-of-adoption decline ~0.603 school-level SD, t+2 around +0.485 SD (≈0.199 and 0.16 student-level SD).

notes.quote: Roughly 62 percent of adopters previously operated under a “no-show” regime, in which students were permitted to keep their phones in backpacks or pockets but were required to keep them out of sight during the school day. An additional 23 percent report having had no formal phone policy at all.
notes.claim: What the pouches replaced: 62% of adopting schools had a lenient "no-show" policy and 23% had no formal policy; only about 23% of adoptions coincided with other major school changes, so this is usually a standalone reform.

notes.quote: Linear mixed models indicated that ban and no ban school groups did not differ significantly in terms of problematic phone use, academic engagement, and school belonging. There was slightly higher bullying in the ban group but bullying decreased significantly in both groups.
notes.claim: South Australia design and results: 1,282 students at baseline and 1,256 at follow-up across five public secondary schools, 2x2 pre-post; ban and no-ban groups did not differ in problematic phone use, academic engagement or school belonging, and there was no condition-by-time interaction on bullying, which fell in both groups.

notes.quote: Being older, a more frequent user of social media, using phone at school before the ban, and experiencing bullying, were associated with phone ban non-compliance.
notes.claim: Compliance and its predictors in South Australia: 87% reported following the ban at baseline; being older, posting on social media more often, having used a phone at school before the ban, and experiencing bullying predicted non-compliance.

notes.quote: Among students aged 12–17 years, there was a 15–18% reduction in bullying incidence following the ban, and a 10–18% reduction among 15- to 17-year-olds.
notes.claim: Spain: two autonomous regions banned phones in schools from 2015; a PISA-based study found a 15-18% reduction in bullying incidence among students aged 12-17 and 10-18% among 15-17 year olds, though PISA limitations prevented conclusive academic findings.

notes.quote: the policy requires students in all government schools to keep their personal devices, including mobile phones, off and away between the start and end of each school day
notes.claim: South Australia's policy scope: devices including phones must be off and away from the start to the end of each school day and during authorised off-site school activities.

notes.quote: If your child is in Grade 7 or older, they can bring a mobile device to school and use it during recess or lunch. If your child is in Grade 6 or younger, they can bring a mobile device to school, but will only be able to use it before and after school.
notes.claim: Ontario's rule is not bell-to-bell: students Grade 7 and above may bring devices and use them at recess or lunch, while students Grade 6 and younger may only use them before and after school.

notes.quote:
This supports student achievement and well-being by:

* keeping students focused on learning by removing distractions
* promoting mental health
notes.claim: Ontario states its aims as keeping students focused by removing distractions and promoting mental health; consequences escalate from handing in the device to the principal's office, consistent with progressive discipline.

notes.quote: Our main result shows that an index of math and Portuguese standardized test scores improved by 0.06 standard deviations in treatment schools relative to control schools after the school-wide ban.
notes.claim: Rio de Janeiro results: test scores improved 0.06 SD in treatment relative to control schools after the school-wide ban, about one fifth of typical annual progression; effects positive in both maths and Portuguese, larger in maths.

notes.quote: Synthesizing this literature, Campbell et al. (2024) reviews 22 studies and concludes that the evidence is inconclusive on whether bans improve academic outcomes or wellbeing, or reduce cyberbullying. A meta-analysis of five studies by B¨ottger and Zierer (2024) reports small positive effects of bans, largely attributable to reductions in bullying rather than gains in achievement.
notes.claim: Two syntheses disagree in emphasis: Campbell et al. review 22 studies and call the evidence inconclusive on academic outcomes, wellbeing and cyberbullying, while Böttger and Zierer's meta-analysis of five studies reports small positive effects of bans, largely attributable to reductions in bullying rather than achievement gains.

notes.quote: Our design does not identify the effect of a phone ban relative to no ban.
notes.claim: The Rio design cannot identify the effect of a ban versus no ban; it identifies a relative contrast across schools with different baseline exposure to the same municipal ban.

notes.quote: Beland and Murphy (2016) document a 0.07 s.d. gain in high-stakes exams, concentrated among low-achieving students in England; Abrahamsson (2026) finds that local phone bans reduced bullying and improved grades and mental health for girls in Norway
notes.claim: The Rio paper's own summary of the quasi-experimental literature: Beland and Murphy 0.07 SD in England concentrated among low achievers; Abrahamsson reduced bullying and improved grades and mental health for girls in Norway; Kessel et al. no impacts in Sweden; and a meta-analysis of five studies reporting small positive effects largely attributable to bullying reductions.

notes.quote: Law No. 15,100/2025, published in the Di´ario Oficial da Uni˜ao on January 13, 2025, prohibits the use of smartphones by students in public and private schools during class time, recess, and other school activities.
notes.claim: Brazil's national ban: Law No. 15,100/2025, published 13 January 2025, prohibits smartphone use by students in public and private schools during class time, recess and other school activities, leaving storage arrangements to schools but requiring consistent enforcement through the school day.

notes.quote: The first is the mobile-free school policy, introduced in January 2024. In the summer of 2024, a representative baseline measurement was conducted.
notes.claim: The Netherlands' mobile-free school policy took effect January 2024; a representative baseline measurement was run in summer 2024; the ministry said it would assess by summer 2025 whether a legal ban was needed, and early results claimed more social interaction and more focused lessons.

notes.quote: The meta-analysis yielded an overall effect size of d = 0.162 (p < 0.05). Smartphone bans have a significant, but modest, effect. This is more pronounced in the domain of social well-being than in the performance domain.
notes.claim: Böttger and Zierer's meta-analysis pooled five quantitative studies and found an overall effect size of d = 0.162 (p < 0.05), larger for social wellbeing than for academic performance.

notes.quote: The answers are best summarised as ‘yes and no’ and ‘not really’.First, there is surprisingly little peer-reviewed evidence about whether phones at school undermine learning
notes.claim: Livingstone's summary of the international evidence on two questions — whether phones disrupt learning, and whether bans produce measurable benefits — is "yes and no" and "not really"; she reports surprisingly little peer-reviewed evidence that phones at school undermine learning.

notes.quote: Another is that the very term ‘ban’ turns out to encompass a multitude of school policies, reflecting different approaches that are often imperfectly and onerously implemented in practice
notes.claim: The "ban" category conceals very different policies, and Livingstone argues that any small benefit from UK school bans was dwarfed by usual and compensatory phone use outside school.

notes.quote: Schools in advantaged contexts tend to have no problem restricting phones because they provide controlled laptops or tablets for learning. But, in less privileged situations, the current panic over phones at school risks halting a long history of valuable, tried-and-tested, and scalable efforts to overcome digital and social divides precisely through the use of phones for learning.
notes.claim: The distributional argument: bans may help disadvantaged children most, but in less privileged settings a blanket restriction risks halting the use of phones for learning where other digital access is lacking.

notes.quote: Despite considerable media attention, remarkably few studies have examined the effects of school smartphone policies on students’academic performance or other outcomes.
notes.claim: The LSE review of reviews: one in seven countries has introduced laws, policies, strategies or guidelines mandating or advising schools to limit or prohibit student smartphone use; remarkably few studies have examined effects; policies vary so much that "ban" is a poor category.

notes.quote: A recent reviews of smartphone policies in the UK classified school responses into four categories, and found that, among secondary schools, 11 per cent implemented what they term an ‘Effective ban’
notes.claim: Even within one country the policy variation is large: among English secondary schools, 11% had an "effective ban", 52% banned phones but allowed them present in bags, 36% had a partial ban, and no school reported no ban at all.

notes.quote: They found that within two years of the policy’s enforcement, students’ PISA scores improved substantially by 10 points in maths and 12 points in science as compared to before the intervention.
notes.claim: The Spanish regional study found PISA scores improved by 10 points in maths and 12 in science within two years — which the LSE review converts to 0.6-0.8 years of learning in maths and 0.72-1.0 years in science.

notes.quote: However, when the authors further explored the results, they found that, when social class, gender and behaviour were controlled for, students in schools with smartphone restrictions had lower achievement across their PISA test scores than schools that permitted smartphone use – although in all models the effect sizes were low.
notes.claim: A counter-result using 2022 PISA data: once social class, gender and behaviour were controlled, students in schools with smartphone restrictions had lower achievement than schools permitting phones, though effect sizes were low in all models — the evidence cannot say which policies work best for whom.

notes.quote: This study examined test scores in secondary school students and found that exam scores improved by an average 0.07 standard deviation in schools that effected a smartphone ban. Significantly, students in the lowest quintile of prior academic achievement made a gain of approximately 14.23% of a standard deviation in exam scores, whereas for high-achieving students in the top quintile, their test scores were unrelated to the ban.
notes.claim: Beland and Murphy's own abstract: exam scores rose 0.07 SD on average after a ban, with the lowest quintile gaining about 14.23% of a standard deviation and the top quintile unaffected — a 15x difference between the average and the bottom-group effect.

notes.quote: Globally, one in seven countries has introduced laws, policies, strategies or guidelines that mandate or advise public schools to limit or prohibit student smartphone use during the school day
notes.claim: Adoption counted differently: the LSE report, drawing on UNESCO 2023, says one in seven countries has laws, policies, strategies or guidelines limiting or prohibiting school smartphone use, and lists the countries — a much lower count than the quarter-of-countries figure cited elsewhere.

notes.quote: We found an absence of randomized controlled trials with evidence resting on a small number of studies with
notes.claim: Campbell et al. found no randomised controlled trials; the evidence rests on a small number of studies differing in design, sample, definition of ban and outcome measures.

notes.quote: positive and significant effects of this policy on the PISA scores of the Galicia region that are equivalent to 0.6–0.8 years of learning in maths
notes.claim: The Spanish PISA gain was found for Galicia specifically, equivalent to 0.6-0.8 years of learning in maths.

notes.quote: A total of 984 students, 302 parents and 42 teachers were initially surveyed in December 2023 about the advantages and disadvantages of the policy.
notes.claim: Dutch pre/post perception study (Radboud, December 2023 to spring 2024): 984 students, 302 parents, 42 teachers surveyed on the "at home or in the locker" policy; most understood it had both benefits and limitations, with one group of students and parents completely resistant.

notes.quote: Betont werden zahlreiche positive Effekte wie ein gestärktes soziales Miteinander, gesteigerte Konzentration und Aufmerksamkeit, eine Reduktion von Cybermobbing aufseiten der Schüler:innen oder die Entschleunigung des Schulalltags.
notes.claim: Austrian accompanying study (interviews, group discussion, survey across policy, authorities, parents, students, teachers) found high support for the ban and reported benefits in social cohesion, concentration and attention, reduced cyberbullying and a slower school day — but also increased phone use outside school, more conflict at home, and parents' safety worries.

notes.quote: Als Nachteile werden eine verstärkte Handynutzung ausserhalb der Schule und damit einhergehende Konflikte im Elternhaus beobachtet.
notes.claim: The Austrian study's reported downsides: intensified phone use outside school and resulting conflict at home, plus parents' safety concerns from reduced reachability and inconsistent enforcement across schools.

notes.quote: If an educator sees a mobile device that is not stored out of view, they will ask it to be handed in for the class (Grades 7-12) or for the day (Grades k-6).
notes.claim: Ontario's enforcement mechanics: students may keep devices but must turn them off or to silent and store them out of view; a device seen not stored is handed in for the class (Grades 7-12) or the day (K-6), and refusal escalates to the principal under progressive discipline.

notes.quote: In Hungary, such regulation took effect on 1 September 2024 under Government Decree No. 245/2024 (VIII. 8.), which designates telecommunication devices as prohibited or restricted items within schools.
notes.claim: Hungary's national restriction took effect 1 September 2024 under Government Decree No. 245/2024 (VIII. 8.), covering phones, tablets, laptops and smartwatches, with occasional teacher- or principal-permitted use; rationale is distraction and cyberbullying. A survey of 1,198 secondary teachers reports the first year's implementation.

notes.quote: Although the effects of MP use have been studied, there has been no systematic review of the MP management research and policies.
notes.claim: The systematic review of school phone policy research and Australian policy documents notes that although effects of phone use have been studied, there had been no systematic review of phone management research and policies — i.e. the policy-design literature is even thinner than the effects literature.

notes.quote: The primary rationale is that mobile phone use distracts students from learning and facilitates cyberbullying.
notes.claim: The comparative review states the mixed-outcome conclusion: banning phones in schools produces mixed outcomes on achievement, wellbeing and cyberbullying exposure.

report.body:
## TL;DR

School smartphone restrictions have spread from a handful of national laws to more than half of countries and roughly two-thirds of US states by 2026, but they are not one policy: "ban" covers bell-to-bell exclusion, phones-in-bags, class-time-only rules and lockable pouches, and evaluations measure different things against different comparisons [16][21]. The best studies agree that restrictions substantially cut phone use in school — teacher-reported in-class personal use fell from 61% to 13% under pouches [16] — while average attainment gains are near zero and precisely bounded [16][12], bullying falls in Norway and Spain but not in the US or Flanders [11][21][16][4], and population mental health does not move in the strongest studies [15][12]. The evidence is quasi-experimental throughout, with no randomised trials [21], and the single most-cited attainment result failed to replicate in Sweden [17]. Bans look justified for reducing in-school phone use and probably bullying, and unjustified as a lever for grades or adolescent mental health.

## Key Findings

- **Adoption is now the norm, but the counts disagree.** UNESCO figures cited in the literature range from one in seven countries [21] to around 40% [5] to one in four [12], rising to more than half of countries and about two-thirds of US states by 2026 [16]. The differences are definitional — laws mandating prohibition versus laws, policies or guidance that advise it.

- **Four distinct regimes are being compared as if they were one.** Bell-to-bell with phones absent or locked (South Australia [10], France, Brazil [17], pouches [16]); bell-to-bell with phones present but out of sight (52% of English secondary schools [21]); instructional time only (Ontario [3], Florida's statute [14]); and partial bans allowing break-time use [21].

- **Restrictions work on phone use itself.** The share of students using phones in class for personal reasons fell from 61% to 13% after pouch adoption, roughly an 80% drop [16]. In England, median in-school smartphone time was 1 hour in permissive schools versus 0.17 hours in restrictive ones [12].

- **But use is displaced, not always reduced.** Students' screen time after school increased to compensate for in-school restrictions, with no difference in problematic usage [5]. This is the strongest explanation on offer for the pattern of nulls downstream.

- **Average attainment effects are zero, and the zero is precise.** The national pouch study can rule out test-score improvements larger than approximately 0.007 student-level standard deviations [16]. Beland and Murphy's English estimate of 0.07 SD, concentrated among low achievers at about 14.23% of an SD [21], did not replicate in Sweden across 1,086 schools [17].

- **Bullying is the most consistent positive finding.** Norway found post-ban bullying decreased among both genders [1][11]; Spain found a 15–18% reduction in bullying incidence among 12–17 year-olds [10][21]. But the US pouch study found no significant change in perceived online bullying (-0.039, SE 0.092) [16], and Flanders found no short-term change in cyberbullying victimisation [4].

- **Population mental health does not move.** Iceland's staggered-adoption study of 70 schools found no meaningful change in depressive symptoms, anxiety or wellbeing [15]. England's SMART Schools study found a wellbeing difference of −0.48 points (95% CI −2.05 to 1.06) on a scale where clinical importance is around 3 [12].

- **Two gender-specific and timing-specific exceptions are real.** Norway found reduced psychological health care use among girls and better GPAs and track placement, especially for disadvantaged girls [11]. The US pouch study found wellbeing falling about 0.603 school-level SD in the adoption year, then rising to about 0.485 SD by year two [16].

- **Enforcement carries its own costs.** Florida saw disciplinary incidents and suspensions jump roughly 25% in the first year of enforcement, falling hardest on Black students [14]. Dutch full bans were associated with lower student-teacher connectedness and, for girls, reduced school belonging [5].

- **The evidence base is thinner than it looks.** No randomised trials exist [21]; a scoping review of 22 studies found incompatible definitions and outcome measures [21]; and several sources cited here summarise the same small set of primary studies.

## Details

### 1. Which jurisdictions have adopted school smartphone restrictions, what the rules actually require, and when they took effect (Ontario, England, the Netherlands, Australian states, France and others)


## Beyond this question

For anyone designing or defending a school phone policy, four things follow from the evidence above.

**Separate the outcomes, because they behave differently.** Bullying is the one outcome where independent studies in different countries agree on a reduction [11][21][10]. Attainment averages are near zero and precisely bounded [16][12]. Mental health at the population level does not move in the best studies [15][12]. A policy case built on better grades and better mental health is not supported; a case built on less bullying and less in-class phone use is.

**Decide which regime you are adopting, and evaluate that.** Ontario's class-time rule [3], England's default-exclusion guidance [2], South Australia's off-and-away day [10] and lockable pouches [16] are four different interventions. The English evidence that restrictive and permissive schools barely differ on most outcomes [12] is evidence about a landscape where 52% of schools were in the middle category, not evidence about bell-to-bell exclusion.

**Budget for the transition.** The US pouch study found wellbeing falling by about 0.603 school-level standard deviations in the year of adoption before recovering to a positive effect by year two [16]. Florida saw suspensions jump by roughly 25% in the first year of enforcement, with the burden falling disproportionately on Black students [14]. Both are predictable costs of enforcement, not evidence the policy failed, and both are avoidable with a grace period and a non-punitive consequence ladder.

**Measure the mediator, not just the outcome.** The single most useful number in this literature is that in-class personal phone use fell from 61% to 13% [16]. A school that cannot say what its policy did to that number cannot interpret its own results.

For researchers, the obvious next study is a within-school randomised or stepped-wedge trial of enforcement intensity, measuring in-class phone use, attention on a lesson task, and bullying as separate outcomes. Nothing in this literature rules that design out; it simply has not been run.

## Open questions

**No randomised trial exists.** Campbell and colleagues found an absence of randomised controlled trials, with evidence resting on a small number of studies that differ in design, sample, definition of ban and outcome measures [21]. Every causal claim here is quasi-experimental.

**Attention has never been measured directly in a ban-versus-no-ban comparison.** The policy literature measures teacher-rated disruption, self-reported classroom attention, or nothing. Sustained attention on a lesson task, mind-wandering rates and time to refocus after interruption have not been measured across policy regimes. The best proxy — self-reported classroom attention in the pouch study — returned an estimate of −0.088 (standard error 0.085), no evidence of change [16].

**The developmental hypothesis is untested.** The claim that growing up with a phone changes attention, sleep or social development is a claim about a decade. The longest outcome windows in this literature are two to three years [14][15], and the pouch study's transition-and-recovery pattern spans two years [16]. No evaluation can yet speak to it.

**Displacement is measured once, in one country.** The finding that students' screen time after school increased to compensate for in-school restrictions, with no difference in problematic usage [5], comes from a single English study. If it replicates, it explains most of the nulls. If it does not, the nulls need another explanation. It has not been replicated.

**The state-by-state Australian picture is unverified here.** New South Wales, Queensland, Western Australia and Tasmania all adopted restrictions, but their primary policy documents could not be read in this pass, so the scope of each rule is not confirmed. The same applies to New Zealand's 2024 regulation, whose primary text I could not retrieve. These are gaps in this report, not findings about the world.

**The counts of adopting jurisdictions do not agree, and the disagreement is definitional.** One in seven countries [21], around 40% [5], one in four [12], and more than half by 2026 [16] cannot all describe the same category. Nobody has published a consistent coding scheme distinguishing laws, guidance, school-level policies and physical interventions.

**Bullying reductions have not been explained mechanistically.** Norway and Spain find reductions [11][21]; the US pouch study and Flanders find none [16][4]; two older studies found cyberbullying more frequent in schools with restrictions [5]. Whether this is measurement (online versus in-person, in-school versus out-of-school) or a real difference in settings has not been tested.

**A caution on the evidence base itself.** Several of the sources cited here are reviews that quote the same underlying studies, sometimes in near-identical language, and the primary studies behind them are few. The apparent weight of agreement across sections 2, 4 and 5 partly reflects a small number of original papers being summarised repeatedly. The independent evidence is thinner than the citation count suggests, and the strongest single results remain Beland and Murphy's English estimate and its Swedish non-replication, Abrahamsson's Norwegian gender split, the English SMART Schools comparison, the Icelandic staggered adoption, the Florida district study and the national pouch study.

q: What did Marshall McLuhan's laws of media (the tetrad) actually claim, how have scholars applied, extended or criticised it since Laws of Media appeared in 1988, and has anyone tried to test it empirically?

report.title: The Tetrad After 1988: What McLuhan's Four Laws Actually Claim, What Scholars Made of Them, and Whether Anyone Has Tested Them
