sentences.sentence: In *Laws of Media* the questions are: what does the artefact enhance, intensify, make possible or accelerate; what does it obsolesce or push aside; what does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier; and what does it flip into when pushed to the limits of its potential [9].
This can be asked concerning a wastebasket, a painting, a steamroller, or a zipper, as well as about a proposition in Euclid or a law of physics" [9].

Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order." Second, that the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process"" [4].
That is why the tetrad is drawn as a square with two rows, and why the application literature routinely describes it as "divided into two areas (ground and figure) with two parts each" [3].
In the 1977 formulation he wrote that "There seems to be only four features, and they are in analogical proportion to each other" [2] — a claim about proportion, not about necessity.

McLuhan presented the four effects as a complement to Aristotle's four causes — material, efficient, formal and final [9] — and the parallel is structural rather than empirical: Aristotle's four answers the question "what makes this thing what it is" from four irreducible standpoints, and McLuhan's four answers "what does this thing do" from four irreducible standpoints.
The reversal law carries the strongest internal logic: "When pushed to the limits of its potential, the new form will tend to reverse what had been its original characteristics" [9].
As Tyler notes, McLuhan's rule was "Never predict anything that hasn’t already happened" [1], which means reversal is supposed to be identified in what has already occurred, not forecast.

Eric McLuhan's preface to the 1988 book states that he and his father "found that everything man\[kind\] makes and does, every procedure, every style, every artefact, every poem, song, painting, gimmick, gadget, theory, technology – every product of human effort – manifested the same four dimensions" [9].

It is on the first page of the book, and it is repeated in the middle of it. *Laws of Media* opens: "This essay offers in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws) observations about the structure and nature of things man makes and does; hence Laws in its title" [5].

Later, the McLuhans credit the criterion directly: "Sir Karl Popper’s (right brain) statement that a scientific law is one so stated as to be capable of falsification made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media" [2].

The subtitle is *The New Science*, and the book's universality claim was stated as a checking procedure: the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [1].

On page 3 the laws are offered in "testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws)"; on page 7, as Guardiani points out, "the "laws" are intended as a "heuristic" device that allows for adjustments and implementations" [10].

Cooper, who worked as McLuhan's graduate assistant for seven years, writes that "For me these are not laws which offer the exactitude of say Newton’s and Boyle’s measurablenatural laws, nor the precision and implementation of Supreme Court rulings, but ratherMcLuhan’s "laws" for me, are novel probing tools which help us rethink media impact from aunique angle of observation" [7].
This is because a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into" [2].

His residual defence is that the laws are generalisations rather than predictions — "The LOM is a generalization or law in that all media obey the same general pattern of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and flip into a complementary form or forms" [2] — which saves the word by removing the content that made it interesting.

The most penetrating assessment of this comes from Basbaum, who puts the problem in Popper's own terms: "It is debatable if the Tetrad model indeed satisfies Popper’s demands, since its testability can be discussed in the same terms Popper dismisses Freudian psychoanalysis theory: it seems to always work, so it is not as falsifiable as the McLuhan claim" [5].

Their abstract states the move plainly: McLuhan's laws "which describe the evolution of artifacts in terms of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal (or flip) are extended to create Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU)" [2].

Logan's own caveats in the same paper are the most important thing in it, and I quoted them in the previous section: the laws are not strictly scientific because they do not yield unique predictions, they are "more of an exploratory tool or probe," and "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM" [2].

Levinson's general lesson from a lifetime of applying the tetrad is the one that matters here, and he states it in a 2020s retrospective: the four effects are rarely singular, and a given medium typically enhances, obsolesces, retrieves and reverses into many things at once [6].
And: "Even McLuhan’s fans rarely devote much energy to the tetrad" [13].

Adam gives the four questions with four secondary citations rather than the 1988 text, applies them quadrant by quadrant with evidence, and concludes honestly that "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions" [3].

The reversal quadrant is pure extrapolation: the smartphone is said to flip into augmented-reality devices like Google Glass, which "might render its users oblivious to their surrounding environment and thus actually restricting human interaction instead of facilitating communication" [3].

The essay's conclusion says the tetrad allows one "to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments" [3], which is exactly the use the fourth law was supposed to be protected from.

Eriksen is sceptical from the start — he calls the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" and says the model needs supplementing [12] — and he improves on the standard application by running tetrads at three separate levels, technological, social and cultural.

It also ends with a sentence that could serve as the epitaph for the whole application literature: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" [12].

The telemedicine literature shows the pattern in a health-services journal, with an explicit method: a qualitative descriptive review of 23 international journals published between 2015 and 2020, mapping telemedicine's documented effects onto the four quadrants [8].

Library and Archives Canada frames the four laws as pedagogical tools, stressing McLuhan's "abiding concern with pedagogy" and describing them as "meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce" [4].
Zingrone, in McLuhan's own circle, extended it to a pentad in 1991 — cited approvingly in *McLuhan Studies* as proof that the "laws" allow for adjustments [10].

"This particular McLuhanesque method is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles: that is, bothersome empiric elements which do not fit the theory are hammered or shorn in order that they be made to fit" [1].

The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit." And at the same time it is too tight: "just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps" [1].
In fact, it is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a set of questions" [1].
Read that way, its value is locative: "The tetrad thus has the potential to help locate a particular technology within the broader technological and cultural environment" [1].

In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and “the occasion”, obsolesces “inhibition”, retrieves “festive spontaneity of speech and gesture”, and reverses into “hangover” and insult" [1].
Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting analysis is ultimately constructive, if the probe works for us, as did the bed for Theseus, rather than against us, as was Procrustes’ lot" [1].

His obsolescence quadrant for digital games asks whether games are displacing television, and he reports Nick Yee's Daedalus Project data: "MMORPG gamers spend on average 21.0 hours per week playing the game … and spend on average 7.7 hours per week watching TV … The national average for TV watching per week is around 28, which is what the above averages add up to" [1].

He notes that the comparison is uncertain, that different studies point different ways, and that "it is clear that more empirical data is indeed needed if we wish to discover what the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing" [1].

If the device is the rigid term, then changes in the plastic terms should be measurable: "Since in the picture here framed the medium device is the least plastic of the three terms [<brain><ap paratus><experience>], one should suppose that the transformations in the very plastic terms "individual experience" and, specially, "neural activity", should be verifiable: we would have accomplished a scientific, falsifiable, demonstration of McLuhan’s thesis" [5].

It is also, by Basbaum's own account, not carried out, and he immediately qualifies it: networked and collective experience undermine the measurability, and he closes by saying that he hopes to have opened directions for "rigorous", "empirical", "hard-science"-like demonstrations in following years, but that "such demonstrations should not be necessary, since changes in culture and society clearly testify, by themselves, how right he was" [5].

Logan and co-authors produce measured intervals between media flips: the alphabet's enhancement, obsolescence and retrieval happen at the outset, "but the flip into print takes 3000 years" [2], and the intervals shorten thereafter through print to computing, the internet, the web and social media.

The telemedicine paper states its method — "a qualitative descriptive by reviewing 23 relevant international journals discussing telemedicine, tetrad, or health services published from 2015-2020" [8] — and then sorts the findings into four boxes.
Logan's concession is explicit: a law of media "does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into" [2].

Iseri and Logan write that "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM" [2], and Adam's application confirms it in practice: "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions" [3].
Levinson's lesson from decades of use is that the four effects are rarely singular and a medium typically does several things in each quadrant [6].

Adam's smartphone tetrad predicts a flip into augmented-reality devices that "might render its users oblivious to their surrounding environment and thus actually restricting human interaction instead of facilitating communication" [3], and her conclusion offers the tetrad as a way "to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments" [3].
McLuhan's own instruction was the opposite — "Never predict anything that hasn’t already happened" [1] — and once a quadrant is licensed to speculate, it cannot fail.
Eric McLuhan is reported to have spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth law and for a single case in which one of the four did not apply, and to have found neither [11].

notes.quote: This particular McLuhanesque method is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles: that is, bothersome empiric elements which do not fit the theory are hammered or shorn in order that they be made to fit.
notes.claim: Tom Tyler (DiGRA 2007, "Play: A Procrustean Probe") names the core objection: applied as a theory, the tetrad risks Procrustean distortion of evidence, forcing empirical details to fit the four boxes.

notes.quote: Applying the tetrad to the human artefact of wine in order to discover its effects on individuals and society, they argue that it enhances “grape juice” (via fermentation), obsolesces “commonplace flavours”, retrieves “ritual observance”, and reverses into “cooking wine vinegar” [21]. Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and “the occasion”, obsolesces “inhibition”, retrieves “festive spontaneity of speech and gesture”, and reverses into “hangover” and insult.
notes.claim: The wine problem: in Laws of Media the McLuhans give two different, incompatible tetrads for wine on the same page, undermining the claim that answers can be checked by "anyone, anywhere, at any time."

notes.quote: Conceived as a universal “scientific method”, the tetrad is far too vague: a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit. At the same time, just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps.
notes.claim: The double bind: the tetrad is simultaneously too vague to be falsifiable (any creative mind can fill the boxes) and too rigid (it compels four answers regardless of evidence).

notes.quote: The idea that these are “scientific laws” in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use the term is preposterous. And yet the tetrad has its uses. In fact, it is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a set of questions:
notes.claim: Tyler's verdict: the scientific-laws claim is preposterous, but the tetrad survives as a heuristic set of questions / probe.

notes.quote: The tetrad thus has the potential to help locate a particular technology within the broader technological and cultural environment.
notes.claim: The defender's concession: divergent tetrad results are tolerable only if the pseudo-scientific rhetoric is dropped; the tetrad's value is locating a technology in its media environment.

notes.quote: The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter. Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting analysis is ultimately constructive, if the probe works for us, as did the bed for Theseus, rather than against us, as was Procrustes’ lot.
notes.claim: Tyler's closing concession — any theory does violence to its subject; it is redeemed only if the analysis is constructive. This is the strongest form of the defence.

notes.quote: Marshall McLuhan’s Laws of Media (LOM), which describe the evolution of artifacts in terms of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal (or flip) are extended to create Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU).
notes.claim: Iseri and Logan (2016) extend the tetrad in two directions beyond McLuhan's artifact-only four laws, adding parallel four-law sets for the environment ("ground") of a medium and for its users.

notes.quote: There is one caveat about the term laws in McLuhan’s Laws of Media, and that is that LOMs are not strictly scientific laws. This is because a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into.
notes.claim: Logan, McLuhan's collaborator, explicitly concedes in a peer-reviewed extension paper that the laws are not strictly scientific laws because they do not yield unique predictions.

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed student-journal application of the tetrad to the smartphone (Adam 2016, Glocality) illustrates the standard post-1988 form of tetrad work: a single analyst's reading that openly concedes multiple interpretations are possible, and that treats reversal only as speculation about the future. No coding scheme, no reliability check, no disconfirming case.

notes.quote:
Published posthumously by his son Eric, _Laws of Media_ (1988) brought together McLuhan's ideas as a concise tetrad of media effects. These four laws of media further exhibit McLuhan's abiding concern with pedagogy: they are meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce. McLuhan phrased them as questions with which to consider any artefact:

1. What does it enhance?
2. What does it make obsolete?
3. What does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier?
4. What does it flip into when pushed to extremes?
notes.claim: Library and Archives Canada's official exhibition gives the four tetrad questions as McLuhan phrased them: enhance, obsolesce, retrieve, and flip into when pushed to extremes — and frames them as pedagogical tools for analysing any artefact.

notes.quote: It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order. The tetrad is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process."
notes.claim: The four laws are meant to hold simultaneously rather than in sequence, and the tetrad is described as an exploratory instrument for the 'grammar and syntax' of artefacts rather than a scientific tool — with the admission that McLuhan himself sometimes spoke of them as successive.

notes.quote: Sir Karl Popper’s (right brain) statement that a scientific law is one so stated as to be capable of falsification made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media
notes.claim: The McLuhans themselves, in Laws of Media p. 93, ground the project explicitly in Popper's falsifiability criterion — the scientific claim is theirs, not an attribution by critics.

notes.quote: There seems to be only four features, and they are in analogical proportion to each other:
notes.claim: McLuhan's 1977 English Journal formulation presents the four features as being in "analogical proportion" to each other — the structural claim behind the tetrad, and the reason the four are not independent variables.

notes.quote: The LOM is more of an exploratory tool or probe that provides insights into the effects of a new medium or technology and its possible evolution, and there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM.
notes.claim: Logan and Iseri's own peer-reviewed position: the tetrad admits multiple correct answers, which is why it cannot be a strict scientific law — a concession from inside the McLuhan camp.

notes.quote: The LOM is a generalization or law in that all media obey the same general pattern of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and flip into a complementary form or forms.
notes.claim: Logan's residual defence of the word "law": it is a universal pattern claim, not a predictive law. This is the reformulation that saves the term by emptying it of predictive content.

notes.quote: The enhancement, obsolescence, and the retrieval all happen at the outset of the arrival of the alphabet or shortly thereafter, but the flip into print takes 3000 years.
notes.claim: The most quantitative-looking claim in the extension literature: measured intervals between flips in the communication chain (alphabet to print 3000 years, print to computing 500, to Internet 24, to Web 21, to social media 5).

notes.quote: Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions.
notes.claim: The standard post-1988 tetrad article: a single analyst's reading, peer reviewed, that openly concedes the answers are interpretation-dependent — no coding scheme, no second coder, no disconfirming case.

notes.quote: This essay offers in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws) observations about the structure and nature of things man makes and does; hence Laws in its title
notes.claim: Basbaum quotes Laws of Media's opening (p. 3) verbatim: the McLuhans explicitly claimed testability and falsifiability as the criteria of scientific laws, and said the title "Laws" was chosen for that reason.

notes.quote: It is debatable if the Tetrad model indeed satisfies Popper’s demands, since its testability can be discussed in the same terms Popper dismisses Freudian psychoanalysis theory: it seems to always work, so it is not as falsifiable as the McLuhan claim.
notes.claim: Basbaum's assessment: the tetrad's testability is debatable in exactly the way Popper dismissed Freudian psychoanalysis — it seems to always work, so it is not as falsifiable as the McLuhan claim.

notes.quote: I expect, however, to have opened some directions based on which we can consider the consequences of McLuhan’s thesis, and that allow us to envision their “rigorous”, “empirical”, “hard-science”-like demonstrations in the following years. Even if, the way I see it, such demonstrations should not be necessary, since changes in culture and society clearly testify, by themselves, how right he was.
notes.claim: Basbaum's own conclusion admits the hard-science demonstration has not been done, and falls back on the claim that such demonstrations "should not be necessary" because cultural change testifies to McLuhan being right — i.e. the retreat from falsification in practice.

notes.quote: Koje se općenite, provjerljive tvrdnje mogu dati o svim medijima?
notes.claim: Silajdžić states the McLuhans' founding question and the universal testability claim in the standard formulation used across the application literature.

notes.quote: Since in the picture here framed the medium device is the least plastic of the three terms [<brain><ap paratus><experience>], one should suppose that the transformations in the very plastic terms “individual experience” and, specially, “neural activity”, should be verifiable: we would have accomplished a scientific, falsifiable, demonstration of McLuhan’s thesis.
notes.claim: The one serious proposal for making the tetrad falsifiable: a triplex isomorphism between brain, apparatus and experience, with the device as least plastic term. Proposed as a research programme, not executed.

notes.quote: Jedna opća lekcija ovdje – jedna od nekoliko općih lekcija oprimjeni tetrade i kako izvući najveću korist od njih – je da su četiri efekta tetraderijetko singularna.
notes.claim: Levinson's general lesson: the four effects of the tetrad are rarely singular; a given medium typically enhances, obsolesces, retrieves and reverses into many things. This is why unique prediction fails.

notes.quote: For me these are not laws which offer the exactitude of say Newton’s and Boyle’s measurablenatural laws, nor the precision and implementation of Supreme Court rulings, but ratherMcLuhan’s “laws” for me, are novel probing tools which help us rethink media impact from aunique angle of observation.
notes.claim: Cooper, who was McLuhan's graduate assistant for seven years, states flatly that the laws do not have the exactitude of Newton's or Boyle's measurable laws, and treats them as probing tools — the standard insider retreat from the scientific claim.

notes.quote: Within the United States the FDA tests all drugs and foods prior to public release. Why not also thoroughly examine and think through the risks and potentialimpact of each new medium and “app” before it is sold to millions?
notes.claim: Cooper's "presearch" remedy: preventive research modelled on the FDA before a medium is released — an admission that the tetrad diagnoses after the fact rather than predicting.

notes.quote: This research method uses a qualitative descriptive by reviewing 23 relevant international journals discussing telemedicine, tetrad, or health services published from 2015-2020.
notes.claim: A peer-reviewed tetrad application with a stated method: qualitative descriptive review of 23 journals 2015–2020, mapping telemedicine onto the four quadrants. The four quadrants are populated from other literature; nothing is tested and no prediction is registered.

notes.quote: What does the artefact ENHANCE or intensify or make possible or accelerate? This can be asked concerning a wastebasket, a painting, a steamroller, or a zipper, as well as about a proposition in Euclid or a law of physics.
notes.claim: The four questions as phrased in Laws of Media (1988), including the explicit claim that the enhancement question "can be asked concerning a wastebasket, a painting, a steamroller, or a zipper" — the universality claim in McLuhan's own words.

notes.quote: McLuhan prescribed his so-called Four Effects (laws of media) as a complementary method to Aristotle’s well-known Four Causes: Material, Efficient, Formal, and Final.
notes.claim: The tetrad's stated intellectual lineage: a deliberate complement to Aristotle's four causes, with the four effects meant to operate simultaneously rather than sequentially.

notes.quote: When pushed to the limits of its potential, the new form will tend to reverse what had been its original characteristics.
notes.claim: The reversal question as worded in the book: the new form "will tend to reverse what had been its original characteristics" when pushed to the limits of its potential.

notes.quote: found that everything man\[kind\] makes and does, every procedure, every style, every artefact, every poem, song, painting, gimmick, gadget, theory, technology – every product of human effort – manifested the same four dimensions.
notes.claim: Eric McLuhan's preface claim: everything made or done manifests the same four dimensions — the universality claim that makes the tetrad falsifiable in principle.

notes.quote: Jorge Luis Borges repeated after Pliny the Elder that there is hardly any book where you cannot find something good. I interpret it today as "there is hardly a bad review without some useful food for thought," a maxim I invented to console myself as I scanned thirty or so reviews of _Laws of Media_.
notes.claim: Guardiani catalogued roughly thirty reviews of Laws of Media for McLuhan Studies; the book's reception was largely dismissive, and he classes many reviews as bad because reviewers refused to try the method.

notes.quote: The socalled tetrads, or four finger exercises, prove nothing.
notes.claim: John Sturrock's New York Times review (26 Feb 1989) dismissed the tetrad outright: "The socalled tetrads, or four finger exercises, prove nothing." The most cited hostile verdict from the mainstream press.

notes.quote: The only objection, and a serious one, that Fekete presents pertains to the "groundlessness" of the number _four_, fixed by the McLuhans as a metaphysically privileged explanatory structure-in effect, as a figure minus a ground-a flaw and contradiction in their argument.
notes.claim: John Fekete's serious objection (Letters in Canada, 1988): the number four is asserted without grounds, making the fourfold a figure without a ground — the deepest structural criticism of the tetrad's necessity.

notes.quote: But to stay within _LOM_, one has only to turn to page 7, and read that the "laws" are intended as a "heuristic" device that allows for adjustments and implementations, as is proved, for example by Frank Zingrone's "pentad" (cf. _McLuhan Studies_ 1, 1991).
notes.claim: The book itself calls the laws a "heuristic" device on p. 7 — the internal admission that undercuts the scientific framing on p. 3, and the passage defenders cite.

notes.quote: Frank Zingrone's "pentad"
notes.claim: Frank Zingrone's 1991 extension to a "pentad" — evidence that the fourfold's number was treated as adjustable by McLuhan's own circle, immediately after publication.

notes.quote: Fekete sees what really counts in _LOM_, "a powerful tool for training awareness" whether or not Popper's theory, invoked by the authors to certify it as scientific, would apply.
notes.claim: Fekete's positive assessment: the tetrad is a tool for training awareness, "whether or not Popper's theory, invoked by the authors to certify it as scientific, would apply" — reception separated the method's value from its scientific certification.

notes.quote: the single biggest intellectual discovery not only of our time, but of at least the last couple of centuries
notes.claim: Eric McLuhan called the tetrad the biggest intellectual discovery of the last couple of centuries, and (per Harman) spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth law and a single counterexample — the strongest evidence that no disconfirming case was ever found or reported.

notes.quote: MMORPG gamers spend on average 21.0 hours per week playing the game … and spend on average 7.7 hours per week watching TV … The national average for TV watching per week is around 28, which is what the above averages add up to.
notes.claim: Tyler's actual empirical engagement on the obsolescence quadrant: Yee's Daedalus data showed MMORPG players averaged 21.0 hours playing and 7.7 hours TV per week against a national TV average around 28 — which he reads as displacement, while cautioning none of the studies is conclusive and more data is needed.

notes.quote: it is clear that more empirical data is indeed needed if we wish to discover what the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing
notes.claim: Tyler's explicit statement that the tetrad's obsolescence claim needs empirical data that does not yet exist — the closest thing in the application literature to a call for a test.

notes.quote: the tetrad is thus divided into two areas (ground and figure) with two parts each
notes.claim: Adam's smartphone tetrad names four sources for its four questions, including Eriksen 1996 and Library and Archives Canada — showing how the application literature relies on secondary restatements rather than the 1988 text itself.

notes.quote: The diversity of responses to its application need not be a problem—once we lose the cod- scientific rhetoric—so long as these provide illuminating insights.
notes.claim: Tyler's remedy: divergent tetrad results are acceptable once the scientific claim is dropped, provided the insights illuminate.

notes.quote: Never predict anything that hasn’t already happened
notes.claim: McLuhan's rule against prediction, quoted by Tyler from Federman: the reversal quadrant is not futurology.

notes.quote: Perhaps the overambitiously phrased and deterministic laws of media can contribute to the creation of distinctions between different kinds of effects; if so, it can be worthwhile to try them out.
notes.claim: Eriksen (1996), an anthropologist, applies the tetrad to the Internet but calls the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" and says the model needs supplementing — and his application layers tetrads at technological, social and cultural levels, which multiplies the interpretive freedom.

notes.quote: The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics.
notes.claim: Eriksen's layered application ends by noting the Internet intensifies, obsolesces, retrieves and flips into identity politics all at once — a demonstration of how the tetrad can be turned to fit, since the same artefact populates every quadrant with the same term.

notes.quote: Yet there is an obvious disjunction between his devotion to the tetrads and the lack of intensity with which others have pursued them.
notes.claim: Harman's diagnosis of the tetrad's reception: despite Eric McLuhan calling it the biggest intellectual discovery of the last two centuries and refusing to retract that, there is an obvious disjunction between his devotion and the lack of intensity with which others pursued it. Even McLuhan's fans rarely devote energy to the tetrad.

notes.quote: Even McLuhan’s fans rarely devote much energy to the tetrad, despite his son’s gripping narrative of how the tetrad was meant to summarize his father’s work as a whole.
notes.claim: Harman: even McLuhan's admirers largely ignore the tetrad, despite Eric's claim that it summarised the whole of his father's work.

notes.quote: The only objection, and a serious one, that Fekete presents pertains to the "groundlessness" of the number _four_, fixed by the McLuhans as a metaphysically privileged explanatory structure-in effect, as a figure minus a ground-a flaw and contradiction in their argument.
notes.claim: Fekete's objection — that the number four is asserted without grounds — is singled out as a serious structural criticism of the tetrad, published in Letters in Canada in 1988, i.e. outside game studies and long before Tyler.

notes.quote: John Sturrock reviewed _LOM_ for _The New York Times_(Feb. 26, 1989) beginning with an ironic pronouncement which, I think, should be taken at face value: "My brain, I realize, is the wrong model for me to be receptive of Marshall McLuhan." What follows is predictable. "The socalled tetrads, or four finger exercises, prove nothing."
notes.claim: The book's immediate reception included a widely noticed hostile verdict in the New York Times (Sturrock, Feb 1989), part of roughly thirty reviews surveyed by Guardiani.

report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. What the tetrad actually claims: the four questions, their provenance, and the logic McLuhan said held them together

The tetrad is four questions that are meant to be asked of any artefact at once, and the first thing to get right is that McLuhan did not present them as a sequence or a checklist. In *Laws of Media* the questions are: what does the artefact enhance, intensify, make possible or accelerate; what does it obsolesce or push aside; what does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier; and what does it flip into when pushed to the limits of its potential [9]. The book's own wording for the first question makes the scope explicit: "What does the artefact ENHANCE or intensify or make possible or accelerate? This can be asked concerning a wastebasket, a painting, a steamroller, or a zipper, as well as about a proposition in Euclid or a law of physics" [9]. A wastebasket and a law of physics are the same kind of object for this purpose, which tells you immediately that the four terms are not meant as variables in a causal model but as aspects under which any made thing can be described.

Library and Archives Canada's exhibition on McLuhan, drawing on the 1988 book, gives the four questions in their plainest pedagogical form — what does it enhance, what does it make obsolete, what does it retrieve that had been obsolesced earlier, what does it flip into when pushed to extremes — and stresses two things about how they work. First, simultaneity: "It is important to remember that these four laws exist simultaneously. Although McLuhan sometimes talked about them as succeeding each other, he did not intend for them to be considered in a chronological order." Second, that the tetrad "is not meant to be a scientific tool, but one for exploration of the "grammar and syntax" of each artefact, a dynamic tool to describe "situations that are in process"" [4]. That framing is worth holding onto, because it is the reading the McLuhan centre itself promoted, and it is in direct tension with the scientific claim the book makes on its opening pages — a tension I take up in the next section.

#### Figure and ground, and why four

The structure behind the four is a pairing, not a list. Enhancement and obsolescence are the figure-level effects — what the new medium brings forward and what it pushes back. Retrieval and reversal are the ground-level effects — what returns from the cultural environment and what the whole configuration turns into at its limit. That is why the tetrad is drawn as a square with two rows, and why the application literature routinely describes it as "divided into two areas (ground and figure) with two parts each" [3]. McLuhan's own explanation of the number is thinner than the structure suggests. In the 1977 formulation he wrote that "There seems to be only four features, and they are in analogical proportion to each other" [2] — a claim about proportion, not about necessity. The four are related to one another the way terms in an analogy are related, which means their number is a property of the analogy rather than something derived from the subject matter.

The stated intellectual lineage reinforces this. McLuhan presented the four effects as a complement to Aristotle's four causes — material, efficient, formal and final [9] — and the parallel is structural rather than empirical: Aristotle's four answers the question "what makes this thing what it is" from four irreducible standpoints, and McLuhan's four answers "what does this thing do" from four irreducible standpoints. The reversal law carries the strongest internal logic: "When pushed to the limits of its potential, the new form will tend to reverse what had been its original characteristics" [9]. That is a claim with content — it says something specific about what happens at extremes — and it is the one quadrant that generates recognisable predictions, from the highway reversing into traffic jams to the car reversing into the traffic accident. It is also the quadrant McLuhan explicitly fenced off from prediction. As Tyler notes, McLuhan's rule was "Never predict anything that hasn’t already happened" [1], which means reversal is supposed to be identified in what has already occurred, not forecast.

#### The universality claim

The most consequential thing the tetrad claims is not any single quadrant but its scope. Eric McLuhan's preface to the 1988 book states that he and his father "found that everything man\[kind\] makes and does, every procedure, every style, every artefact, every poem, song, painting, gimmick, gadget, theory, technology – every product of human effort – manifested the same four dimensions" [9]. The publisher's description of the book carried the same claim in a sharper form: anything that does not contain answers to the four questions is not the product of human creation.

That is a very strong claim, and it has an unusual logical shape. It is not the claim that most media show these four effects but that all human artefacts do, without exception. A universal claim of that form is falsifiable in principle by a single counterexample, which is why the search for one matters so much to the tetrad's standing — and, as I show in section 5, Eric McLuhan is reported to have spent much of his later career looking for one and never reported finding it. It is also why the claim is unfalsifiable in practice: the tetrad's defenders can always fill a recalcitrant quadrant by reinterpreting a term, and the critics' complaint is that this is what always happens.

#### What the four questions are not

Three clarifications matter for reading everything that follows.

The questions are not content questions. McLuhan's whole point is that the effects of a medium are not the effects of what it carries, so a tetrad of television is not a list of programmes. This is the tetrad's genuine gain: it forces attention onto the operation of the artefact rather than its message.

The questions are not predictive in the ordinary sense. Obsolescence does not mean extinction — McLuhan's own observation that there is more handwriting now than before print is the standard illustration — and reversal is retrospective. A tetrad that reads as a forecast has been misused, which is the most common failure in the applied literature.

And the four are not independent. Because they are "in analogical proportion," filling one quadrant constrains the others, and the same historical relation between a new medium and an old one will typically appear in obsolescence, retrieval and reversal at once. The fourfold's appearance of covering four separate dimensions is misleading: it is one configuration described from four angles. That is a strength for a probe and a weakness for a measurement instrument, because four boxes filled from one insight look like four findings.

### 2. The scientific claim and its retreat: Popper, the 1975 launch, the Venable exchange, and the wine problem

The scientific claim was not foisted on McLuhan by critics. It is on the first page of the book, and it is repeated in the middle of it. *Laws of Media* opens: "This essay offers in testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws) observations about the structure and nature of things man makes and does; hence Laws in its title" [5]. Later, the McLuhans credit the criterion directly: "Sir Karl Popper’s (right brain) statement that a scientific law is one so stated as to be capable of falsification made it both possible and necessary to formulate the laws of media" [2]. The subtitle is *The New Science*, and the book's universality claim was stated as a checking procedure: the four questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" [1]. Anyone assessing the tetrad has to start from the fact that its authors entered the falsifiability contest voluntarily and on Popper's terms.

#### The 1975 launch

The first public airing was in *Technology and Culture* in 1975, in an article titled "McLuhan's Laws of the Media." McLuhan presented the four laws as hypotheses and invited readers to try to disprove them, describing them as representing an ordering of thought and experience which had not yet been disproved. The framing was Popperian in spirit — a conjecture offered for refutation — and the journal was the right venue for it, since *Technology and Culture* was where historians of technology argued about how to study technology. The move put the tetrad in front of exactly the readership best equipped to test it.

That readership took him up on it, and the result is the most direct empirical challenge the tetrad has faced. In 1976 the journal published two critical pieces, "Flaws in McLuhan's Laws" and "Misunderstanding the Media's Laws," the latter by William Henry Venable, an engineer and lawyer who read the four laws through C. S. Peirce's logic of signs and argued that the four terms presuppose a single target that technologists have always aimed at — a version of the charge that the tetrad smuggles in a telos. I could not obtain the full texts: both sit behind JSTOR's paywall, and no open copy appears to exist. What is available is McLuhan's published reply, and it is more revealing than the critique.

Faced with a reader who took the testability claim literally, McLuhan moved the ground. He wrote that the tetrads are analogical — that there are no connections between any of them, only dynamic ratios — and that there was no point of contact between the four terms. This is a striking reply for a book that opens by promising falsifiable observations. If there are no connections between the four quadrants, then nothing about one quadrant can contradict anything about another, and the structure cannot be refuted by showing that a proposed relation fails. The 1976 exchange therefore marks the first retreat from the scientific claim, and it happened in the same journal that published the claim, within a year of it.

#### The internal contradiction

The retreat is also inside the book. On page 3 the laws are offered in "testable and falsifiable form (the criteria of scientific laws)"; on page 7, as Guardiani points out, "the "laws" are intended as a "heuristic" device that allows for adjustments and implementations" [10]. The two pages cannot both be right. A heuristic device that admits adjustment is not a falsifiable law, and a falsifiable law does not admit adjustment when a case fails.

The same contradiction recurs wherever the McLuhan circle states its position. Cooper, who worked as McLuhan's graduate assistant for seven years, writes that "For me these are not laws which offer the exactitude of say Newton’s and Boyle’s measurablenatural laws, nor the precision and implementation of Supreme Court rulings, but ratherMcLuhan’s "laws" for me, are novel probing tools which help us rethink media impact from aunique angle of observation" [7]. Logan, McLuhan's collaborator and the most persistent academic extender of the tetrad, concedes the same point in a peer-reviewed paper: the laws "are not strictly scientific laws. This is because a LOM does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into" [2]. His residual defence is that the laws are generalisations rather than predictions — "The LOM is a generalization or law in that all media obey the same general pattern of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and flip into a complementary form or forms" [2] — which saves the word by removing the content that made it interesting. A pattern that every medium obeys, with no constraint on which particular things are enhanced, retrieved or flipped into, is not a law in any predictive sense.

The most penetrating assessment of this comes from Basbaum, who puts the problem in Popper's own terms: "It is debatable if the Tetrad model indeed satisfies Popper’s demands, since its testability can be discussed in the same terms Popper dismisses Freudian psychoanalysis theory: it seems to always work, so it is not as falsifiable as the McLuhan claim" [5]. That is the correct comparison. Popper's objection to psychoanalysis was not that its claims were false but that they were unfalsifiable — the theory could accommodate any clinical outcome. The tetrad accommodates any artefact, and its own authors demonstrated this on the same page, twice.

#### What survives the retreat

The retreat is not a defeat, and it is worth being precise about what remains.

What is lost is the claim to be science in Popper's sense: unique predictions, checkable by anyone, with specified conditions under which the laws fail. No defender of the tetrad now makes that claim in an unqualified form, and the peer-reviewed literature has largely converged on the heuristic reading.

What survives is a structured set of questions with three real virtues. It directs attention to the operation of a medium rather than its content, which is genuinely corrective in a field that studies messages. It organises historical material by forcing the analyst to say what a new medium displaced and what it brought back, which is a useful discipline even when the answers are contested. And the reversal law in particular generates recognisable, checkable observations about what happens at extremes, which is why it is the quadrant most often used with effect.

The cost of the retreat is that the tetrad becomes unfalsifiable by its defenders' own account and must be judged by other means — whether the analysis illuminates, whether it corrects a specific misconception, whether it survives comparison with a rival tetrad of the same artefact. That is a legitimate standard for an essay and a poor one for a research programme, because it is applied after the fact by the person who did the analysis.

### 3. How scholars have applied and extended it since 1988: Logan's laws of media environments, Levinson's tetrad wheels, Harman's object-oriented reading, and the design and media-ecology literature

The literature since 1988 divides into five strands, and they do different things: formal extension of the tetrad's scope, chaining tetrads through time, philosophical reconstruction, application to new artefacts, and use as a design or policy instrument. The volume of application is much larger than the volume of extension, which is itself a finding — the tetrad gets used far more than it gets tested or improved.

#### Formal extension: laws of environments and users

The most systematic extension comes from Robert Logan, who collaborated with McLuhan at the University of Toronto, working with students and co-authors in *Philosophies*. Iseri and Logan take the original laws of media (LOM) and add two parallel four-law sets: Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU). Their abstract states the move plainly: McLuhan's laws "which describe the evolution of artifacts in terms of enhancement, obsolescence, retrieval, and reversal (or flip) are extended to create Laws of Media Environments (LOME) and Laws of Media Users (LOMU)" [2].

The motive is a real gap. McLuhan's four laws ask what a medium does; they do not ask what happens to the environment in which the medium operates, nor what happens to the people who use it. LOME and LOMU fill those in by running the same four questions at a different level — a move that is structurally sensible and that also multiplies the tetrad's interpretive freedom, because there are now three nested fourfolds to fill and no rule governing how they interact.

Logan's own caveats in the same paper are the most important thing in it, and I quoted them in the previous section: the laws are not strictly scientific because they do not yield unique predictions, they are "more of an exploratory tool or probe," and "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM" [2]. This is an insider's concession published in a peer-reviewed journal by McLuhan's own collaborator, and it is decisive for the empirical question. If more than one answer to each question is correct, there is nothing to test.

#### Chaining: Levinson's tetrad wheels

Paul Levinson organised the 1978 tetrad conference — before the book appeared — and has been the tetrad's most consistent expositor since. His contribution is temporal: the idea of tetrad wheels, which chain tetrads through time so that the reversal of one medium becomes the enhancement of the next. This addresses a genuine weakness. A single tetrad is a snapshot; media evolution is a sequence; and the wheel makes the sequence analysable without abandoning the four-term structure.

Levinson's general lesson from a lifetime of applying the tetrad is the one that matters here, and he states it in a 2020s retrospective: the four effects are rarely singular, and a given medium typically enhances, obsolesces, retrieves and reverses into many things at once [6]. That is a description of how the tool behaves in skilled hands, and it is also the reason unique prediction fails. If the television tetrad legitimately has several enhancements, several obsolescences and several reversals, then any particular observation is compatible with the tetrad and with its negation.

Levinson also supplies the most candid account of the Popper connection. According to the Lindia and Levinson article in *New Explorations*, McLuhan joked about adopting Popper, and Levinson glosses the joke as meaning that if the laws of media are capable of falsification they can't do too much damage. I have this only secondhand, from a record document summarising excerpts; the article itself was not reachable. But the gloss is consistent with everything else in the record: the Popper framing was adopted as protective colouring rather than as a research commitment, by someone who understood what falsification would require.

#### Philosophical reconstruction: Harman and the object-oriented reading

The most ambitious attempt to give the tetrad philosophical foundations is Graham Harman's chapter "The McLuhans and Metaphysics" in *New Waves in Philosophy of Technology* (2009). Harman begins from the reception problem rather than the theory: Eric McLuhan called the tetrad the biggest intellectual discovery of the last two centuries and never retracted it, yet there is "an obvious disjunction between his devotion to the tetrads and the lack of intensity with which others have pursued them". And: "Even McLuhan’s fans rarely devote much energy to the tetrad" [13]. That is the most accurate one-sentence description of the tetrad's scholarly standing that I found anywhere.

Harman's constructive move is to universalise the tetrad further than the McLuhans did: it should apply to all objects, not only human artefacts, since in his object-oriented ontology every object is a medium. This removes the awkward boundary at "things man makes" but makes the falsifiability problem worse, because the domain is now everything.

His more useful contribution is a test for fourfolds in general. A rigorous fourfold, on his account, comes from crossing two dualisms, and warns that even frivolous fourfolds can be generated — his example is daytime eating, daytime drinking, night-time eating, night-time drinking. The constraint is that the underlying dualisms must be profound enough to generate the four terms rather than being imposed on them. He identifies the tetrad's dualisms as figure/ground and metamorphosis. This is the only serious criterion anyone has proposed for distinguishing a good tetrad from a decorative one, and it is a philosophical criterion, not an empirical one: it tells you whether the fourfold is well-formed, not whether its contents are true.

Harman also supplies a reading with real analytical payoff. On his account the enhancement quadrant flips into the appearance of inevitability, so that an extension of man silently murders other possible worlds. Read this way the tetrad is a counterfactual engine that argues against technological determinism rather than for it, since each enhancement is accompanied by a record of what it foreclosed. That is a more defensible McLuhan than the standard deterministic reading, but it is Harman's reconstruction, not McLuhan's text.

#### Application: the largest and weakest strand

The application literature is enormous and mostly of one type: a single analyst runs the four questions on a new artefact and publishes the result. The peer-reviewed specimen I read in full is Isabelle Adam's 2016 *Glocality* essay on the smartphone, which is a fair representative and is more careful than most. Adam gives the four questions with four secondary citations rather than the 1988 text, applies them quadrant by quadrant with evidence, and concludes honestly that "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions" [3].

What is missing is instructive. There is no coding scheme, no second coder, no reliability estimate, no pre-specified disconfirming observation, and no comparison with a rival tetrad. The reversal quadrant is pure extrapolation: the smartphone is said to flip into augmented-reality devices like Google Glass, which "might render its users oblivious to their surrounding environment and thus actually restricting human interaction instead of facilitating communication" [3]. That is a forecast, and McLuhan's own rule was against forecasting. The essay's conclusion says the tetrad allows one "to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments" [3], which is exactly the use the fourth law was supposed to be protected from.

The anthropologist Thomas Hylland Eriksen's 1996 web essay on the Internet, identity politics and the laws of media is a better application, and it shows both the method's power and its licence. Eriksen is sceptical from the start — he calls the laws "overambitiously phrased and deterministic" and says the model needs supplementing [12] — and he improves on the standard application by running tetrads at three separate levels, technological, social and cultural. The result is genuinely illuminating about identity politics. It also ends with a sentence that could serve as the epitaph for the whole application literature: "The Internet intensifies identity politics, renders identity politics obsolete, retrieves identity politics and may flip into identity politics" [12]. When the same term populates all four quadrants, the tetrad has not distinguished anything; it has absorbed everything.

The telemedicine literature shows the pattern in a health-services journal, with an explicit method: a qualitative descriptive review of 23 international journals published between 2015 and 2020, mapping telemedicine's documented effects onto the four quadrants [8]. This is the most methodologically explicit application I found, and it is still a mapping exercise — the quadrants are populated from other studies, nothing is predicted, and no observation could have come out otherwise.

#### The design and policy strand

The most active current use is not scholarly at all. The tetrad has become a design and strategy instrument: workshops, consulting frameworks, product critiques, pedagogy. Library and Archives Canada frames the four laws as pedagogical tools, stressing McLuhan's "abiding concern with pedagogy" and describing them as "meant to be used as tools to analyze the patterns of effects that different technologies produce" [4]. The *Explorations in Media Ecology* "Probes" section institutionalises the same use, publishing short exploratory items rather than test results.

The design use has a real logic — the four questions force a product team to name what a new feature displaces and what it brings back, which is more than most product reviews do — and it has no evidential standard at all. A tetrad workshop produces insight, not findings. Chris's own record contains several documents built on exactly this use, including a tetrad of the digital calendar and to-do app, a tetrad of surveillance pricing, and a proposed "Tetrad Court" in which rival tetrads are argued adversarially. That last idea is, as far as I can find, the only proposal anywhere for making the tetrad produce something checkable: it does not test the tetrad, but it does make the disagreement between rival tetrads visible and force each quadrant to carry evidence. It has not been built.

#### What the extensions have in common

Across all five strands, the same three moves recur, and none of them addresses the empirical problem.

First, the scope is always widened — to environments, to users, to all objects, to every level of analysis — which increases the tetrad's reach and decreases its testability.

Second, the scientific claim is always retained in softened form. Logan keeps the word "law" while conceding it makes no unique predictions; Harman keeps the fourfold while substituting a metaphysical for an empirical criterion; the design literature keeps the authority of "laws" while using them as prompts.

Third, the fourfold's number is treated as adjustable. Zingrone, in McLuhan's own circle, extended it to a pentad in 1991 — cited approvingly in *McLuhan Studies* as proof that the "laws" allow for adjustments [10]. A structure whose number of terms can be increased by a colleague within three years of publication is not a structure that is claiming necessity.

The extensions are real contributions: Logan's levels, Levinson's chains, Harman's dualism criterion and Eriksen's layered analysis all make the tetrad more useful. None of them makes it more testable, and several make it less.

### 4. The criticism: the Procrustean double bind, determinism, the wine example, and what defenders concede

The most sustained critique of the tetrad as a method was published not in a media-studies journal but in game studies. Tom Tyler, then a senior lecturer in philosophy and culture at Oxford Brookes, opened his 2007 DiGRA paper "Play: A Procrustean Probe" with the myth of Procrustes — the bandit who stretched short guests and cut down tall ones to fit his bed — and used it as a warning about what the four laws do to evidence. "This particular McLuhanesque method is itself in danger of operating according to Procrustean principles: that is, bothersome empiric elements which do not fit the theory are hammered or shorn in order that they be made to fit" [1].

#### The double bind

Tyler's objection is more interesting than the usual "it's vague" complaint, because it runs in two directions at once. As a universal method the tetrad is too loose: "a sufficiently creative mind can imagine, for almost any human artefact, a huge range of things which it might be considered to augment, obsolesce, retrieve, and reverse into. The laws of media do not lend themselves to falsifiability at all, since empirical examples can readily be stretched to fit." And at the same time it is too tight: "just like Procrustes’ bed, McLuhan’s tetrad is unrelentingly rigid: it requires us to fill the gaps" [1]. A schema that can absorb any evidence and that also compels four answers whether or not the evidence exists is in trouble in both directions simultaneously. Fluency in filling the boxes is not evidence of anything, because the schema guarantees that the boxes will be filled.

His verdict on the scientific claim is blunt: "The idea that these are “scientific laws” in anything like the sense in which we ordinarily use the term is preposterous." But he does not throw the tetrad out. "And yet the tetrad has its uses. In fact, it is best conceived, as McLuhan himself often did, as a set of questions" [1]. Read that way, its value is locative: "The tetrad thus has the potential to help locate a particular technology within the broader technological and cultural environment" [1]. The gain is not prediction but placement — forcing attention onto how an artefact operates rather than onto what it carries, and organising a field's scattered findings so that, in McLuhan's phrase, you can see where you have been barking up the wrong tree.

#### The wine problem

The critique's strongest single piece of evidence comes from inside the book. On one page of *Laws of Media*, the McLuhans run the tetrad on wine twice and get two different answers. In the first version, wine enhances grape juice by fermentation, obsolesces commonplace flavours, retrieves ritual observance, and reverses into cooking wine vinegar. "Or, at least, these are the answers the first time they apply the tetrad. In an alternative version on the same page, we find that wine enhances food and “the occasion”, obsolesces “inhibition”, retrieves “festive spontaneity of speech and gesture”, and reverses into “hangover” and insult" [1].

Both tetrads are plausible. Neither is checkable against the other. This matters because the book's own universality claim is precisely that the questions "can be asked (and the answers checked) by anyone, anywhere, at any time, about any human artefact" If the two authors, working on the same page about the same artefact, produce incompatible tetrads, the checking procedure is not doing the work the claim requires. Tyler's inference is that if the authors cannot agree with themselves, it seems unlikely that anyone else reliably will.

#### What the defenders concede

The defence Tyler offers is worth stating carefully, because it is also the most defensible position in the literature. It has three parts.

First, drop the scientific pretension and the diversity of results stops being a defect. Divergent tetrads for the same artefact are a problem only for a method that promised uniformity. Once the tetrad is a heuristic, a spread of readings is what a good heuristic produces.

Second, redefine the terms so they do real work. Tyler treats obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction — television is repurposed, not replaced — and confines reversal to potentials already present rather than forecasts, since McLuhan himself urged never to predict anything that hasn't already happened. He also narrows his own scope deliberately, restricting enhancement to solo-play complexity rather than attempting what he calls potentially Procrustean taxonomies of play.

Third, accept that any schema does violence to its subject and ask whether the violence paid off: "The danger with any theory or schema is that it inevitably does violence to its subject matter. Such violence is redeemed only if the resulting analysis is ultimately constructive, if the probe works for us, as did the bed for Theseus, rather than against us, as was Procrustes’ lot" [1]. That is a pragmatic test, not a truth test, and it is the strongest thing that can be said for the tetrad on its own terms.

#### The charges the tetrad does not answer

Three criticisms survive even the charitable reading.

The first is that the pragmatic test is unfalsifiable in practice. "Did the analysis turn out constructive?" is a judgement made after the fact by the person who did the analysis. There is no independent scorer, no comparison with an analysis that did not use the tetrad, and no case in the literature where an analyst ran a tetrad, found it unconstructive, and reported that result. A test that no outcome can fail is not a test.

The second is the determinism charge. The four laws describe what a medium does to a culture, and the doing is attributed to the medium's form. The McLuhans' own rhetoric — "the medium is the message" — invites the reading that human choice is downstream of technological form. Tyler's remediation fix helps here, because remediation implies human agents deciding what to carry forward, and the figure/ground reading of the tetrad as a counterfactual engine (asking what possible worlds an extension silently killed) pushes in the same direction. But this is a repair, not what the book says.

The third is that the tetrad's four terms are not independent. Obsolescence, retrieval and reversal are all, in practice, statements about the same relation between a new medium and an older one, seen from different angles. That is not fatal for a heuristic, but it does mean the fourfold's appearance of completeness is misleading: filling four boxes may be one insight described four ways. The only published attempt I found to supply a rigorous criterion for a fourfold — Graham Harman's demand that a valid fourfold be generated by crossing two profound dualisms — is a philosophical constraint, not an empirical one, and it is Harman's own construction rather than the McLuhans'.

### 5. Has anyone tested it empirically? What has been attempted, what a test would require, and what remains unmeasured

No. I searched the application literature, the media-ecology journals, the extension papers, the critical literature and the citation indexes, and I found no study that tests the tetrad as a hypothesis. What exists is a large body of applications, one partial empirical check inside a critical paper, one proposed experimental programme that was never carried out, and a scattering of quantitative-looking claims that turn out to be retrospective.

This is a negative finding, so it is worth stating how I looked. I read in full: Tyler's DiGRA paper, Adam's *Glocality* essay, Basbaum's *ARS* paper, Iseri and Logan's *Philosophies* article, Eriksen's tetrad essay, Guardiani's review-of-reviews in *McLuhan Studies*, Cooper's *New Explorations* piece, Silajdžić's application article, and the telemedicine tetrad paper. I searched Semantic Scholar, Crossref, OpenAlex and the free web indexes for tetrad-plus-test, tetrad-plus-coding, tetrad-plus-reliability, and tetrad-plus-empirical, and checked the *Explorations in Media Ecology* and *New Explorations* contents. The pattern was consistent: every hit was an application, a commentary, or a theoretical extension.

#### The one place a tetrad claim meets data

Tyler's paper is the only tetrad application I found that takes a quadrant and checks it against a dataset. His obsolescence quadrant for digital games asks whether games are displacing television, and he reports Nick Yee's Daedalus Project data: "MMORPG gamers spend on average 21.0 hours per week playing the game … and spend on average 7.7 hours per week watching TV … The national average for TV watching per week is around 28, which is what the above averages add up to" [1]. The arithmetic is neat — the two figures add up almost exactly to the national average he cites — and Tyler reads it as displacement.

He then does what almost no one else in this literature does: he refuses to overclaim. He notes that the comparison is uncertain, that different studies point different ways, and that "it is clear that more empirical data is indeed needed if we wish to discover what the enhancement of digital play is at the same time obsolescing" [1]. He also redefines obsolescence as remediation rather than extinction to accommodate the contrary evidence, which is intellectually honest and also the exact move that makes the tetrad unfalsifiable: when the data does not show displacement, obsolescence is redefined so that it does not have to.

Even taken at face value, this is a check on one quadrant of one tetrad, not a test of the tetrad. It shows that a claim derived from the obsolescence quadrant is consistent with a dataset. It does not show that the tetrad predicted the number, that a rival framework would not have predicted it equally well, or that anything in the theory would have been refuted by a different number.

#### The proposed programme that was never run

The most serious attempt to specify what a falsifying test would look like comes from Sérgio Basbaum, in an *ARS* paper whose title states the ambition: "Scientificizing McLuhan." Basbaum's proposal is a "triplex isomorphism" between three terms — brain, apparatus and experience — with the medium as the least plastic of the three. If the device is the rigid term, then changes in the plastic terms should be measurable: "Since in the picture here framed the medium device is the least plastic of the three terms [<brain><ap paratus><experience>], one should suppose that the transformations in the very plastic terms "individual experience" and, specially, "neural activity", should be verifiable: we would have accomplished a scientific, falsifiable, demonstration of McLuhan’s thesis" [5].

That is a genuine experimental design, and it is the only one in the literature. It is also, by Basbaum's own account, not carried out, and he immediately qualifies it: networked and collective experience undermine the measurability, and he closes by saying that he hopes to have opened directions for "rigorous", "empirical", "hard-science"-like demonstrations in following years, but that "such demonstrations should not be necessary, since changes in culture and society clearly testify, by themselves, how right he was" [5]. That final move is the retreat from falsification in its purest form: here is how one could test the theory, the test has not been run, and it does not need to be run because the outcome is already known.

#### Quantitative-looking claims that are not tests

Two bodies of work look empirical and are not.

Logan and co-authors produce measured intervals between media flips: the alphabet's enhancement, obsolescence and retrieval happen at the outset, "but the flip into print takes 3000 years" [2], and the intervals shorten thereafter through print to computing, the internet, the web and social media. These are real historical durations, but they are assigned after the fact. Nothing in the tetrad specifies in advance how long a flip should take, so no observed interval could contradict it. The numbers illustrate the framework; they do not test it.

The applied literature produces quadrants populated from cited studies, which reads as empirical grounding but is a mapping exercise. The telemedicine paper states its method — "a qualitative descriptive by reviewing 23 relevant international journals discussing telemedicine, tetrad, or health services published from 2015-2020" [8] — and then sorts the findings into four boxes. The boxes are filled from the literature rather than from the tetrad, and no observation was capable of coming out otherwise.

#### Why no one has tested it

Four obstacles are visible in the literature itself, and they are stated by the tetrad's friends rather than its enemies.

First, there are no unique predictions. Logan's concession is explicit: a law of media "does not make unique predictions as to what is retrieved from the past or what complementary form the technology or medium will flip into" [2]. Without a unique prediction there is no risky test, because any outcome is compatible with the framework.

Second, there is more than one correct answer. Iseri and Logan write that "there is often more than one correct answer to the four questions posed by the LOM" [2], and Adam's application confirms it in practice: "Naturally, multiple interpretations are possible when applying the tetrad, since one’s interpretation is always based on own thoughts and perceptions" [3]. If two analysts can both be right while disagreeing, inter-coder reliability — the first requirement of any coding instrument — is undefined.

Third, the effects are plural even in a single competent application. Levinson's lesson from decades of use is that the four effects are rarely singular and a medium typically does several things in each quadrant [6]. Multiply plural answers by four quadrants and any observation confirms the tetrad.

Fourth, the reversal quadrant is used as prophecy, which puts it outside checking. Adam's smartphone tetrad predicts a flip into augmented-reality devices that "might render its users oblivious to their surrounding environment and thus actually restricting human interaction instead of facilitating communication" [3], and her conclusion offers the tetrad as a way "to try to predict – or at least speculate – about future developments" [3]. McLuhan's own instruction was the opposite — "Never predict anything that hasn’t already happened" [1] — and once a quadrant is licensed to speculate, it cannot fail.

The decisive piece of evidence that no test has occurred is negative but strong. Eric McLuhan is reported to have spent the rest of his life looking for a fifth law and for a single case in which one of the four did not apply, and to have found neither [11]. If the tetrad's most devoted exponent conducted a lifetime search for a disconfirming case and never announced one, then either no case exists or no result was ever reported — and in either situation the tetrad has no published failure record to weigh.

#### What a real test would require

The literature does not contain a specification, so what follows is my inference from the obstacles above rather than a finding.

A testable version of the tetrad needs five things that no application has supplied.

Pre-specified content. Before examining the artefact, the analyst must state what the four quadrants will contain, in terms specific enough to be wrong — not "ritual" but a named practice, not "community" but a named institution.

Independent coding. At least two analysts coding the same artefact from the same protocol, with a reliability statistic reported. If the tetrad cannot produce agreement above chance between trained coders, it is a private instrument.

A disconfirming observation. Each quadrant needs a stated observation that would falsify it, registered in advance. For obsolescence, a medium that gains adoption while its supposed obsolescent target holds steady would count; Tyler's displacement question is exactly the right shape, and the fact that he had to redefine obsolescence when the data was uncertain is exactly the failure mode to guard against.

Rival tetrads, compared. Since the same artefact admits multiple correct tetrads, the test is not whether a tetrad fits but whether one tetrad predicts better than another. This is the wine problem turned into a design: generate both McLuhan tetrads for wine, state what each predicts, and see which the record supports.

A prediction ledger. Each quadrant's claims get a dated, checkable consequence, scored later. This is the only way to convert a retrospective framework into a prospective one, and it is the design this record has independently arrived at in its own proposal for a probe ledger with dated, resolvable stakes.

The cheapest real test available is not the neuroscience programme Basbaum sketches. It is a reliability study: take twenty artefacts, train ten analysts on the four questions with defined terms, have them code independently, and report agreement. That study would take a few weeks, would cost almost nothing, and has apparently never been done. Its result would settle more about the tetrad's status than any further essay, because a fourfold that different trained readers cannot apply consistently is not a method — and one that they can is worth testing properly.

## Open questions
