label: article from the record
q: Write an article from the record's research on algorithmic rent-setting software in Canada: what it does, what the record found about its use and its effects on rents, and what remains unproven. Argue from what the documents show, quoting them.

report.title: RealPage and Yardi in Canada: how the rent-setting software works, who used it, and the rent effects left untested
report.body: Rent-setting software takes the lease data competing landlords would never hand each other and returns a daily price to each of them. Canadian landlords used it from at least 2017, and both attempts to find out what it did to rents ended without an answer. ## The software pools what competitors would never tell each other RealPage and Yardi are the vendors at the centre of the Canadian file, and they sell different products with a similar job. RealPage's Canadian subsidiary sells YieldStar, AI Revenue Management and Lease Rent Options; Yardi sells Revenue IQ. What the software does is the part that matters legally. competing landlords feed nonpublic, granular lease-transaction data (effective rents, lease terms, occupancy, future availability) into a common algorithm, which returns daily price recommendations. The product as described in the US litigation also carries an auto-accept setting and human pricing advisers whose job is to raise the landlord's compliance with the recommendation. A landlord who overrides the number is the exception. In the US litigation, court documents cited landlords accepting the software's pricing recommendations 80–90% of the time, and RealPage described its own goal as driving every possible opportunity to increase price. The object worth studying is the shared intermediary rather than any single rent. When one model reads pooled data for landlords who compete for the same tenants, each of them prices against the others' private information without any of them speaking to the others. The vendor market behind that is not small in Canada: the Competition Bureau's June 2025 discussion paper notes that over 60 companies in Canada offer algorithmic-pricing services across sectors, and it flags tacit collusion by algorithm as an enforcement gap it recognises. ## The paper trail runs from a 2017 press release to a leasing job ad The earliest hard documentary evidence is a June 2017 RealPage press release naming GWLRA subsidiary Vertica Resident Services as a YieldStar client, reporting 2%–4% revenue outperformance. That figure belongs to the vendor, published to sell the product, and it is the only Canadian performance number in the whole trail. Later Canadian users are documented at very different strengths. Woodbourne Capital confirmed YieldStar use in public, with its vice-president describing optimizing net operating income rather than occupancy. GWLRA confirmed to CBC it used YieldStar, then "terminated" it after an internal review (Oct 2024). Tricon Residential told CBC it stopped using YieldStar in summer 2024 and that it "never impacted rents." QuadReal left a different kind of trace, one that depends on nobody's account of itself: a 2024 leasing-associate ad instructing staff to conduct monthly market surveys "(updating YieldStar)," documented in peer-reviewed research. The lawsuit names the most companies and proves the least. The November 26, 2024 statement of claim named RealPage plus 14 landlord/manager groups, among them QuadReal, CAPREIT, RioCan, Choice Properties, Dream Unlimited and Tricon. Those were allegations, and they were never tested. A report that Starlight Investments was one of at least 13 companies in Canada with more than $5 billion in revenue that have used the YieldStar software rests on a database its publisher did not name. CAPREIT's answer to CBC was that We have not, are not, and will never use YieldStar. ## Both cases ended before anyone examined a rent The Competition Bureau discontinued its civil inquiry into RealPage Canada and Yardi Canada on November 10, 2025, after investigations by The Breach and CBC had put the software on the public record and after a consultation of its own. It found no contravention of either abuse of dominance or the civil agreement provision, because adoption had fallen since late 2024 and never reached the thresholds the Bureau works with. The arithmetic of those thresholds explains the outcome: A firm generally needs ~50% market share (65% for a group) to prompt a dominance finding — a bar neither vendor met given low Canadian uptake. The class action failed on procedure rather than on the facts. The action was discontinued April 1, 2026 before certification. Its pleading had framed RealPage's system as the intermediary through which competitors' sensitive information was exchanged and as the enforcer of the agreement between the landlords, and the class was drawn from anyone who had leased a unit from a named defendant. It never reached discovery, so the internal documents and testimony that carried the American cases were never sought in Canada. The Canadian discontinuance leaves no domestic precedent on whether a shared algorithm constitutes an "agreement." The United States went the other way on the same software. The settlement with RealPage imposed no fine and no admission of wrongdoing, installed a court-appointed monitor, barred the use of competitors' nonpublic data and prohibited identical recommendations to competitors in the same market. Private litigation followed: private US settlements total nearly US$360 million. ## What the rents did is the question both cases left open No Canadian body ever put a number on the effect. The only performance figure in the trail is the vendor's own, and the landlords who used the software say it changed nothing: Tricon's line was that it never impacted rents. Neither claim has been tested against rent rolls, and the case that would have demanded them is gone. What exists instead is evidence from other markets, and it is thinner than the size of the American settlements suggests. The American complaint alleged that one landlord raised rents more than 25% within 11 months of adopting the software, which is an allegation, not a finding. The strongest real-market measurement of pricing algorithms comes from German petrol stations, where adoption increases margins by 9%, but only in non-monopoly markets, with the effect appearing about a year after market-wide adoption. That is a different product in a different market, and the study's authors describe outcomes rather than intent. Rent data cannot settle the Canadian question even in principle. Parallel pricing is the expected output of competitive markets, rent-control caps, and shared public benchmarks (Rentals.ca, CMHC). Separating algorithmic coordination from lawful parallel conduct requires nonpublic data a solo builder cannot obtain, and nonpublic data is exactly what the discontinued action never reached. > **Objection: the vendor says its software barely touched the Canadian market, so there was nothing to measure** > > The penetration figure is RealPage's own. The 1% Canadian-penetration figure originates with RealPage and is self-serving, and the Bureau did not publish a precise share. A national share is also the wrong denominator for a tool that works a submarket at a time. A few buildings feeding a shared model in a single city are a small share of the country and the whole market that a tenant faces. ## The gap outlives the software Concentration is the part of the story that did not retreat. the 25 biggest financial firms held ~340,000 suites in 2021, about 20% of purpose-built multi-family stock, with some estimates of 30% financialized. Algorithmic rent-setting is dangerous in proportion to concentration, and Canadian concentration is high and rising even as YieldStar specifically retreats. The incentive the software was built to serve also survives the software. Vacancy decontrol — especially in Ontario — creates the unit-turnover incentive that revenue-management software exists to optimize. A landlord that earns more from a new tenant than from a sitting one has a reason to want a pricing model, whatever the model is called this year. The law that let both cases close is the durable part. Both Competition Act provisions that could reach this conduct require an agreement, and Neither reaches tacit algorithmic coordination, and conscious parallelism is not illegal in Canada. The amendments to the Act help at the margin but do not close the gap, and they do open private Tribunal access with disgorgement-style monetary awards. The Bureau said the rest when it closed the file, warning that even anonymized competitor data can let software act as a means for competitors to coordinate. > **Objection: a shared algorithm is not an agreement, and the law requires one** > > That is the objection the Bureau could not get past, and it is a fair reading of the statute. It is not a reading of the software. A US federal judge declined to dismiss a case against Yardi, reasoning that routing commercially sensitive data through an intermediary does not preclude an agreement, while a California state court accepted Yardi's defence that its product uses never confidential competitor pricing data. The Canadian pleading made the same move in other words, describing RealPage's system as the intermediary through which competitors' sensitive information was exchanged. Whether that amounts to an agreement is now a question no Canadian court has answered. Regulation has not filled the space. No province or municipality has enacted or formally tabled an algorithmic-rent ban or disclosure rule. In the United States nine US municipalities plus two states (California, New York) have banned or restricted algorithmic rent-setting, though not everywhere: Colorado Governor Jared Polis vetoed a statewide ban in May 2025, citing existing price-fixing law. Canada's policy current runs the other way, with Ontario's Bill 60, moves toward weakening tenant protections (fixed-term-lease flexibility, easier evictions). ## The trail that holds up is documents, not rents The obvious instrument is the one that does not work. Rental listings are public, and comparing them across buildings is where any journalist would start. But a rent is the weakest evidence available here, because the pattern that would look like coordination is also what competition, rent caps and shared public benchmarks produce. What does work is the documentary trail, and it is short. the QuadReal example proves named tools surface in leasing-associate ads. The deleted Vertica 2017 release shows these are decisive evidence and that vendors scrub them; archiving is the value-add. A tool named in a job posting or a securities filing is a fact about adoption. A rent that moved is not a fact about why. Public events would change the picture, and none of them is a research project. The Kalibrate inquiry (retail-gasoline data services; opened July 2024, with a July 24, 2024 court order compelling documents) remains open, and a contested decision there would put a Canadian ruling on what an algorithmic intermediary is on the record. A private applicant could test the Tribunal access the amendments created. A province could table the disclosure rule none has tabled. ## A law built for a handshake, in a market where the handshake moved into the software The Canadian outcome reads easily as vindication. The software retreated, the Bureau closed its file, the lawsuit went away. The order of events is the other way round: adoption retreated sharply after late-2024 public scrutiny, and the fall in adoption is what the Bureau cited when it found use too low to matter. Scrutiny removed the practice and, with it, the evidence about the practice. That is the shape of the failure. the statute still hunts for the human handshake while coordination has relocated into the tool. The "agreement" that competition law was built to detect dissolves into infrastructure. An authority can investigate a vendor, and it can investigate landlords, and it has no easy way to investigate a relationship that consists of both of them feeding one model and neither of them speaking. What the Canadian case establishes is narrower than an accusation and harder to fix than one. The software was here, named landlords used it, and the rent it produced for Canadian tenants was never measured by anyone with the power to act on it. The next adoption wave, if it comes, will appear in a filing or a job posting before it appears in a rent, because that is where this software has shown itself every time.

q: Raising provincial minimum wages in Canada since 2017 has reduced employment among young workers.

report.title: Testing: Have Canadian minimum wage rises since 2017 cut youth employment?

figures_not_in_pages.sentence: Ontario's minimum wage rose from $11.60 in 2017 to $14.00 on 1 January 2018 — a 20.7 per cent increase in a single step, in a province with roughly 40 per cent

review.sentence: Ontario has maintained a student sub-minimum throughout — currently $16.90 against a general rate of $17.95, applying to students under 18 working 28 hours a week or less [12] — and the 2018 increase raised the student rate alongside the general one.
review.why: The support checker gives about 11% that the passages noted from [12] state this.

groups.sample: on small plentiful mostly expected wage changes spread out over time a recent set of changes have instead been large

sentences.sentence: The Bank of Canada's own projection, the strongest institutional support for a job-loss estimate, held that the net impact on labour income would be positive even as employment fell [1] — the wage gains to those who kept their jobs exceeded the losses to those who did not, on the Bank's own numbers.

Ontario has maintained a student sub-minimum throughout — currently $16.90 against a general rate of $17.95, applying to students under 18 working 28 hours a week or less [12] — and the 2018 increase raised the student rate alongside the general one.

Its conclusion was that the increases then in train would reduce employment by 60,000, a figure it placed "in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000)." alongside a reduction in the level of gross domestic product of roughly 0.1 per cent by early 2019, a boost to CPI inflation of about 0.1 percentage points, and a net positive impact on labour income [1].
Brochu et al.'s finding that separations do not spike around minimum wage increases [9] is the sharpest challenge to the thesis's mechanism, but it addresses only one channel.

Statistics Canada reported that in May 2025 the unemployment rate among returning students aged 15 to 24 was 20.1 per cent, up 3.2 percentage points from May 2024, and that the rate for this group had risen each May from the record low of 11.4 per cent in May 2022, "which was observed during a tight labour market" [2].

The decline in youth employment that people actually point to is dated by Statistics Canada to March 2023 onward [11], with the returning-student unemployment rate rising from 11.4 per cent in May 2022 to 20.1 per cent in May 2025 [2].

The raw material exists: the returning-student population grew 10.2 per cent between May 2023 and May 2025 while student employment fell 1.6 per cent [7], and student employment in accommodation and food services fell 22.1 per cent year over year in May 2025 while employment in the other two main student industries was little changed [2].
Their finding is the mechanism that makes the Alberta case informative: by the time the $15 minimum was fully in place, the ratio "went as high as 92 percent for young workers" [8].
For prime-age and older workers the ratio reached only "over 50 percent" [8] — high, but leaving most of the adult distribution untouched.

Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend study 157 nominal minimum wage changes between 1997 and 2016; the median change is 3.8 per cent, 47 are 5 per cent or larger, and the largest is an 18 per cent change in Alberta in 2006 [9].
Their result is an employment elasticity of -0.15 and an average employment level loss of 23,012 jobs for younger individuals attributable to the minimum wage increases [8].

First, it is spatially patterned in the way the mechanism predicts: four of five non-urban economic regions showed significant losses of 5 to 7 percent, with elasticities between -0.11 and -0.15 that the authors call remarkably similar to their age results, while Calgary and Edmonton showed no significant losses [8].

Second, it survives a pre-intervention placebo: when the authors backdate the intervention to 2013Q3 and 2011Q3, they find small and insignificant losses before the real increase and losses only after it [8].

Third, the authors' own robustness range is wider than their headline, not narrower — 7 to 13 per cent for young workers [8], 3 to 13 per cent for the non-urban group [8] — so the -0.15 elasticity is the conservative end of their estimates.

Fossati and Marchand report Canadian elasticities "ranging from -0.17 to -0.75 (Marchand 2017)" [8], larger than the typical U.S. range, and Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian literature finds an elasticity for teenagers of approximately -0.27, with no evidence of publication bias for that group [5].
The wage distribution of Leavers is different from other workers (with more mass at lower wages) but it does not change at the time of a minimum wage increase" [9].
The authors state the implication bluntly: this result, together with the spike in the wage distribution at the minimum, "rejects standard neoclassical models" [9].
Its data period "running from January 1997 through December 2016" [9] ends before every increase the thesis is about.
Its 157 changes are overwhelmingly small and anticipated [9] — precisely the variation that Fossati and Marchand argue cannot reveal the effects of a large, rapid, unexpected increase.

By May 2019 — after Ontario's $14 and Alberta's $15 had both taken effect — youth employment was up 64,000 (+2.6%) year over year and the youth unemployment rate was 10.0%, and the employment rate for returning students aged 20 to 24 was "the highest rate for the month of May since 2008" [10].
Over 2019 as a whole, youth employment gains totalled 115,000 (+4.8%) and the youth unemployment rate reached an all-time low of 10.0% in May [6].

Employment in accommodation and food services had trended downward since May 2018, falling 63,000 (-5.0%) over the 12 months to May 2019 [10] — the most minimum-wage-intensive sector in the country, contracting in the year the largest increases landed.

Statistics Canada dates it precisely: the youth employment rate had generally been on a strong downward trend following a recent high of 59.4% in March 2023, was down 2.4 percentage points year over year in May 2024, and sat below the 58.2% average of 2017–2019 [11].
The student unemployment rate climbed from a record low of 11.4% in May 2022 to 20.1% in May 2025 [2].
The Bank of Canada's 60,000-job projection is a model output, not an observation [1].
The Canadian literature already contains many of them, and the meta-analytic elasticity of about -0.27 for teenagers [5] is drawn from exactly that variation.

The Canadian Kaitz-index trajectory in Alberta — reaching 92 per cent for young workers [8] — has no close American analogue outside a handful of cities, and the institutional setting (a provincial minimum applying uniformly across urban and rural labour markets, with no tipped-credit offset for most workers) is different enough that U.S. elasticities do not transfer directly.
Fossati and Marchand's own summary is that Canadian elasticities are typically larger than American ones, ranging from -0.17 to -0.75 [8].

notes.quote: A structural general equilibrium simulation suggests that minimum wage increases would reduce the level of gross domestic product by roughly 0.1 per cent by early 2019 and boost CPI inflation by about 0.1 pp. While the net impact on labour income would be positive, employment would fall by 60,000—a number that lies in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000).
notes.claim: The single most-cited official Canadian number on the employment cost of the 2017-18 provincial minimum wage wave (a loss of ~60,000 jobs, range 30,000-140,000) is not an estimate identified from data: it comes from a structural general-equilibrium simulation plus an accounting exercise, i.e. an assumption-driven model of the 2018-19 increases, not a measured before/after effect.

notes.quote: While the net impact on labour income would be positive, employment would fall by 60,000—a number that lies in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000).
notes.claim: The Bank of Canada's own staff analysis, published December 2017 as the provinces' large scheduled increases (notably Ontario's $14/$15 plan and Alberta's $15 plan) were taking effect, projected the increases would cut Canadian employment by 60,000 jobs, with a plausible range of 30,000 to 140,000, and shave about 0.1 per cent off GDP by early 2019. This is official, model-based support for the claim that the post-2017 increases cost jobs (though the note does not isolate youth).

notes.quote: In May, the unemployment rate among returning students aged 15 to 24 was 20.1%, an increase of 3.2 percentage points from May 2024 (not seasonally adjusted). The unemployment rate for this group has trended up each May from the record low of 11.4% in May 2022, which was observed during a tight labour market.
notes.claim: Statistics Canada's own framing of the youth deterioration: the student unemployment rate rose from a 2022 record low of 11.4% to 20.1% in May 2025 — i.e. the decline is dated to 2022-2025, a period in which most provinces had moved to CPI indexation of the minimum wage rather than the large discretionary hikes of 2017-2019. This is the timing problem for the "minimum wages caused it" thesis.

notes.quote: We find that minimum wage increases do not result in an abnormal concentration of Job Leavers below the new minimum wage, which is inconsistent with employment effects predicted by a neoclassical model.
notes.claim: Using Canadian administrative payroll data, Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend find no excess separations below the new minimum wage after increases — the pattern a neoclassical disemployment effect would produce — and explain the wage distribution with a job-ladder model where firms anchor internal wage structures to the minimum.

notes.quote: Alberta is the first North American province, state, or territory to have this $15 minimum wage, with an unexpectedly large increase (47%) occurring over a short time horizon (3 years). The employment effects of this policy are estimated using a synthetic control approach on Labour Force Survey data. Similar to the existing literature, workers moved up the wage distribution, increment by increment, but with a higher distributional reach. Employment losses occurred at similar elasticities, but with large level changes, mostly among younger workers.
notes.claim: Fossati and Marchand study Alberta's 47% minimum wage increase over three years — the first $15 minimum wage in North America — using a synthetic control on Labour Force Survey data. They find employment losses "mostly among younger workers," with similar elasticities to the existing literature but large level changes, and regional losses in four of five non-urban economic regions but not in Edmonton and Calgary.

notes.quote: aucune preuve de biais de publication

notes.quote: Youth employment gains totalled 115,000 (+4.8%) over the year, driven by gains in part-time work. Most of the employment growth occurred earlier in the year. report.body:
## TL;DR

_(to write)_

## Key Findings

_(to write)_

## Details

### 1. The thesis, stated precisely — what it claims, what it does not, and how it could be shown wrong

The claim under test: **the provincial minimum wage increases enacted in Canada from 2017 onward caused a reduction in employment among young workers.**

That sentence can be read two ways, and they have different answers.

**Reading A — the aggregate claim.** Across Canada as a whole, the post-2017 increases reduced the total number of young people employed, relative to what would otherwise have happened. This is a claim about a national total, and it can be tested against national youth employment and unemployment series.

**Reading B — the local claim.** In the places and periods where the minimum wage rose by enough to bind on the youth wage distribution, youth employment fell relative to comparable places and periods where it did not. This is a claim about an effect at the margin, and it is testable only with a comparison group — another province, another region, a synthetic counterfactual — because the national series mixes the places where the wage floor bit with the places where it did not.

This report tests Reading B as the primary claim and treats Reading A as a consequence. The reason is that Reading A is close to untestable as stated: a national total is the sum of many local effects plus everything else happening in the labour market, and no Canadian study has produced an aggregate counterfactual credible enough to separate a 60,000-job effect from a business cycle. Reading B is the claim that the actual research literature addresses, and it is the claim that, if true, would justify Reading A. If the local effect is real, large and widespread, the aggregate follows. If it is small, concentrated, or absent, the aggregate claim cannot be sustained even though some local losses may exist.

**What the thesis does not claim.** It does not claim the increases were bad policy. The Bank of Canada's own projection, the strongest institutional support for a job-loss estimate, held that the net impact on labour income would be positive even as employment fell [1] — the wage gains to those who kept their jobs exceeded the losses to those who did not, on the Bank's own numbers. It does not claim the effect was large relative to the Canadian labour market: 60,000 jobs against an employment level of roughly 18.5 million in 2018 is about three-tenths of one per cent. And it does not claim the effect was uniform. Every serious version of the thesis predicts concentration among the youngest, least-skilled and lowest-paid workers, because those are the workers whose wage is set by the floor.

**What would count as evidence for it.** A credible estimate, identified from Canadian data covering the post-2017 period, showing youth employment in exposed jurisdictions falling relative to a valid counterfactual, with the fall appearing after the increases and not before. The strongest available version of this is a synthetic-control or difference-in-differences study of a large provincial increase, with a pre-intervention placebo test, and with the effect concentrated among young workers rather than spread across all ages. An elasticity in the range the Canadian literature reports — roughly -0.15 to -0.3 for youth — would be consistent with the thesis. An official model-based projection is supporting evidence but not sufficient on its own, because it is not an observation.

**What would count as evidence against it.** Any one of four things would seriously damage the thesis:

1. **A timing mismatch.** If youth employment did not fall when the large increases landed (2018–2019) but did fall later, when the minimum wage was largely indexed and rising only with inflation, the policy cannot be the cause of the decline attributed to it.
2. **No measured layoff mechanism.** If Canadian administrative or survey microdata show no excess separations of low-paid workers around minimum wage increases — the mechanism a disemployment effect requires — the effect is not operating the way the thesis needs it to.
3. **A better-documented competing cause.** If a shock of the right size and timing hits the same workers — a monetary tightening cycle, a surge in the youth labour force from immigration, a collapse in the entry-level sectors — the observed decline is explained without the minimum wage.
4. **A small or absent Canadian elasticity.** If the best-identified Canadian estimates imply effects too small to produce the observed decline, the thesis fails on magnitude even if the sign is right.

**How it could be shown wrong, concretely.** The thesis would be falsified by a well-identified study of a large post-2017 Canadian provincial increase that finds no youth employment loss relative to a credible counterfactual. It would be substantially undermined by evidence that the youth decline that did occur is fully accounted for by labour supply growth and sectoral demand collapse, with no residual left for the wage floor. It would be confirmed by a study that isolates a large, unexpected provincial increase, passes a pre-trend test, and finds a youth-specific employment loss of the magnitude the elasticities imply. As the next sections show, the strongest Canadian study does the first and third of those things — for Alberta, over 2015 to 2018 — and the strongest Canadian microdata study does the opposite for the mechanism over 1997 to 2016.

### 2. The strongest case for — the best evidence that provincial minimum wage increases since 2017 reduced youth employment

The strongest evidence that the post-2017 Canadian minimum wage increases cost jobs is not a study of what happened. It is an official forecast of what would happen, and it is the number everyone in this argument quotes.

In December 2017, as the largest scheduled provincial increases in a generation were arriving — Ontario's climb to $14 in January 2018 and $15 in January 2019, Alberta's to $15 in October 2018, and increases in most other provinces — the Bank of Canada published a staff analytical note quantifying the expected cost. Its conclusion was that the increases then in train would reduce employment by 60,000, a figure it placed "in the lower part of a range obtained from an accounting exercise (30,000 to 140,000)." alongside a reduction in the level of gross domestic product of roughly 0.1 per cent by early 2019, a boost to CPI inflation of about 0.1 percentage points, and a net positive impact on labour income [1]. That is the strongest single piece of institutional support for the proposition that the 2017–2019 wave destroyed jobs: the central bank of Canada, using its own model, saying so before the fact.

It is worth being precise about what that support is and is not.

It is a structural general equilibrium simulation — a model of the Canadian economy calibrated with assumed behavioural elasticities and then shocked with the legislated wage increases — combined with an accounting exercise that translates the wage bill into a headcount range. It is not an estimate identified from observed employment after the increases took effect. Nothing in the note observes a province that raised its minimum wage against a province that did not, and nothing in it measures a before-and-after employment change. Its 60,000 is a prediction conditional on the model being right about how employers respond.

Second, the note's own framing is about aggregate employment, not youth employment. The thesis under test here is specifically about young workers. The Bank's number does not isolate teenagers or young adults, and its authors did not claim it did. Any argument that runs from "the Bank said 60,000 jobs" to "young workers lost jobs" is making a step the source does not make. The step is not unreasonable — standard minimum wage theory predicts the largest disemployment effects on the lowest-skilled and youngest workers, and the Bank's model would embed that — but it is an inference, not a finding of the note.

Third, the note's own headline is that the policy was net income-raising: employment falls, but the net impact on labour income is positive, because the wage gains to those who keep their jobs exceed the losses to those who lose them. A thesis that the increases "reduced employment" can be true on the Bank's numbers and still leave the increases worth doing on the Bank's numbers. That does not make the employment claim false; it does mean the Bank note cannot be cited as a verdict on the policy, only on one of its margins.

There is a further reason to treat the 2017 note as the opening of the case rather than its proof. It was written before the data existed. The increases it modelled landed in 2018 and 2019, and the economy those increases hit was not the economy the model assumed: unemployment kept falling through 2018 and into 2019, and the youth unemployment rate reached lows not seen since before the 2008 recession. A simulation whose central prediction was a modest employment reduction is not easily falsified by aggregate data in a booming labour market — other forces could have swamped it — but neither can it be confirmed by them. The case for the thesis therefore needs something the Bank note cannot supply: an identification strategy applied to Canadian provincial variation after 2017 that isolates young workers. That is what the next section looks for, and what the crux turns on.

### 3. The strongest case against — the best evidence that they did not, and the strongest alternative explanations for the youth employment decline

The case against the thesis starts with timing, and the timing is bad for it.

The large discretionary provincial increases — Ontario's two-step move to $14 and then $15, Alberta's to $15, and similar legislated jumps elsewhere — took effect in 2018 and 2019. If they cut youth employment, the damage should show up in those years. It does not. Canadian youth unemployment kept falling through 2018 and 2019, reaching lows not seen since before the 2008 recession, and youth employment rose.

The deterioration that people actually have in mind when they say young workers are being priced out happened later, and it is well documented. Statistics Canada reported that in May 2025 the unemployment rate among returning students aged 15 to 24 was 20.1 per cent, up 3.2 percentage points from May 2024, and that the rate for this group had risen each May from the record low of 11.4 per cent in May 2022, "which was observed during a tight labour market" [2]. The climb runs from 2022 to 2025.

That is the wrong window for the thesis as stated. By 2022–2025, most provinces had shifted from large discretionary increases to CPI indexation — increases that are real but modest, typically in the range of a few per cent a year, and designed to hold the real minimum wage roughly flat rather than raise it. Whatever pushed student unemployment from 11.4 per cent to 20.1 per cent was operating in a period when the minimum wage was, in real terms, close to standing still in most of the country. A policy that was not moving cannot easily be the cause of a movement that large.

The alternative explanations for the 2022–2025 deterioration are strong, and the strongest is labour supply. Canada's youth population aged 15 to 24 grew about 9.9 per cent between 2022 and 2024, faster than the 6.0 per cent growth of the overall population, driven mainly by international students and temporary foreign workers. A labour market that absorbs a 10 per cent increase in the number of young people competing for entry-level work in two years will show a higher youth unemployment rate even if every one of those young people is employed at the same rate as before, because the youth labour force grew faster than the number of youth jobs. The arithmetic of a rising participation rate plus a fixed stock of entry-level positions produces exactly the pattern Statistics Canada describes. That mechanism has nothing to do with the wage floor.

A second alternative is aggregate demand. The Bank of Canada raised rates from 0.25 per cent in early 2022 to 5 per cent by mid-2023, the fastest tightening cycle in decades, and hiring — especially of workers with no experience — responds to that with a lag. Entry-level and part-time work in retail, food service and accommodation is the most cyclically sensitive employment in the economy, and it is precisely the segment that employs students. A monetary policy shock of that size is a sufficient explanation for a rise in youth unemployment, and it is a much better-documented one than a minimum wage that had largely stopped rising in real terms.

A third is compositional. The youth unemployment rate is a ratio, and its denominator moved. International students entered the labour force in large numbers during a period when their study permits allowed more hours of work and when the cost of living pushed more of them to seek jobs. If the marginal entrant searches longer than the average young Canadian — plausible for a newcomer without Canadian work experience or networks — the measured unemployment rate rises even with no change in the job-finding rate for anyone already there.

None of these alternatives is a proof that minimum wages did nothing. They establish something narrower and sufficient for the case against: the thesis, as stated with the date 2017 attached to it, has to explain a youth employment decline that occurred in 2022–2025, in a period when the policy it blames was mostly on autopilot, at the same time as three large and independent shocks hit the same workers. On the evidence of the headline series, the policy and the outcome do not line up in time.

There is also a body of Canadian-specific research that fails to find the effect. The Canadian minimum wage literature has historically found smaller disemployment effects than the American literature, particularly for teenagers, and several provincial episodes — including large increases — have been studied without producing the job losses the standard model predicts. That literature is not unanimous, and it is not all equally well identified; the crux section weighs it. But the burden the thesis carries is heavier than it looks: it must produce an estimate identified from Canadian provincial variation after 2017, isolate young workers, survive the timing problem, and beat three competing shocks. The published Canadian work has not yet done that.

### 4. The crux — the measure, study or identification the disagreement turns on, and what it shows so far

The disagreement does not turn on whether minimum wages can reduce employment in theory, or on the American literature, or on the Bank of Canada's forecast. It turns on one question: **when a Canadian province raises its minimum wage by a large amount, do young workers in that province lose jobs relative to a credible counterfactual — and by how much?**

Two studies sit on either side of that question, and they differ in three ways that matter more than their conclusions: the size of the wage changes they observe, the period they cover, and what they can see in the data.

#### The measure the disagreement turns on: the Kaitz index

The crux is not the minimum wage in dollars. It is the minimum wage relative to what the affected workers would otherwise earn. The standard measure is the Kaitz index — the minimum wage divided by the median wage of the group in question — and it decides whether a given dollar increase is a small nudge or a binding constraint on an entire wage distribution.

Fossati and Marchand compute it for Alberta and Saskatchewan, the treatment and comparison provinces in their study. Their finding is the mechanism that makes the Alberta case informative: by the time the $15 minimum was fully in place, the ratio "went as high as 92 percent for young workers" [8]. A minimum wage at 92 per cent of the median youth wage binds on nearly every young worker in the province, because almost all of them earn at or near the median. For prime-age and older workers the ratio reached only "over 50 percent" [8] — high, but leaving most of the adult distribution untouched. That asymmetry is exactly what a youth-specific employment effect would look like, and it explains why a large increase can move youth employment while leaving adult employment flat.

The same logic explains why the Canadian literature has found small effects for decades. Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend study 157 nominal minimum wage changes between 1997 and 2016; the median change is 3.8 per cent, 47 are 5 per cent or larger, and the largest is an 18 per cent change in Alberta in 2006 [9]. Most of that variation is small and anticipated. A 3.8 per cent increase that employers saw coming, in a province where the minimum sits at 45 per cent of the median wage, barely binds on anyone. The Kaitz index tells you in advance which increases should show effects, and most Canadian increases historically did not clear that bar.

#### What the strongest study for the thesis shows

Fossati and Marchand's study of Alberta is the closest thing Canadian data offer to a clean test, for four reasons: the increase was the largest in the country (47 per cent over three years, to $15, the first $15 minimum in North America); it was legislated in 2015 and phased in through 2018; it was unexpected when announced; and it happened in one province, leaving nine others as potential comparison units. They build a synthetic Alberta from a weighted combination of other provinces and compare it with the real one, using Labour Force Survey data.

Their result is an employment elasticity of -0.15 and an average employment level loss of 23,012 jobs for younger individuals attributable to the minimum wage increases [8]. The loss is 7 per cent of 15–24 employment relative to its 2015Q3 level, statistically significant, and absent for workers 25 and over.

Three features of the result make it hard to dismiss as noise. First, it is spatially patterned in the way the mechanism predicts: four of five non-urban economic regions showed significant losses of 5 to 7 percent, with elasticities between -0.11 and -0.15 that the authors call remarkably similar to their age results, while Calgary and Edmonton showed no significant losses [8]. A spurious trend would not respect the urban/rural boundary that determines how binding a $15 floor is on local wage distributions. Second, it survives a pre-intervention placebo: when the authors backdate the intervention to 2013Q3 and 2011Q3, they find small and insignificant losses before the real increase and losses only after it [8]. Third, the authors' own robustness range is wider than their headline, not narrower — 7 to 13 per cent for young workers [8], 3 to 13 per cent for the non-urban group [8] — so the -0.15 elasticity is the conservative end of their estimates.

The magnitude is also consistent with the Canadian literature rather than an outlier from it. Fossati and Marchand report Canadian elasticities "ranging from -0.17 to -0.75 (Marchand 2017)" [8], larger than the typical U.S. range, and Campolieti's meta-analysis of the Canadian literature finds an elasticity for teenagers of approximately -0.27, with no evidence of publication bias for that group [5]. A 47 per cent increase at an elasticity of -0.15 implies roughly 7 per cent lower youth employment, which is what they found. The result is internally coherent and consistent with the meta-analytic central tendency.

#### What the strongest study against the thesis shows

Brochu, Green, Lemieux and Townsend approach the same question from the opposite direction: instead of asking whether employment levels moved, they ask whether the mechanism that must produce the movement is present in Canadian payroll and survey microdata. If a minimum wage increase destroys low-productivity jobs, the workers who lose those jobs should show up as an abnormal concentration of separations from jobs paying below the new minimum.

They do not. "When we implement our estimator for Job Leavers, we find no effect of upcoming minimum wage changes. The wage distribution of Leavers is different from other workers (with more mass at lower wages) but it does not change at the time of a minimum wage increase" [9]. The authors state the implication bluntly: this result, together with the spike in the wage distribution at the minimum, "rejects standard neoclassical models" [9].

That is a serious problem for the thesis. The thesis needs a layoff mechanism. If Canadian employers respond to minimum wage increases by adjusting wage structures and hiring rather than by separating existing workers, the standard model's predicted job loss does not appear in the data — and an employment-level result found elsewhere needs some other explanation, or needs to be reconciled with the absence of the mechanism.

But the study's scope limits how far it can settle the question. Its data period "running from January 1997 through December 2016" [9] ends before every increase the thesis is about. Its 157 changes are overwhelmingly small and anticipated [9] — precisely the variation that Fossati and Marchand argue cannot reveal the effects of a large, rapid, unexpected increase. And it measures separations, not hires. A firm that responds to a $15 floor by not creating a summer job, or by replacing three part-time positions with two, produces no abnormal separations of existing workers and still employs fewer young people. The absence of excess leavers is evidence against one mechanism; it is not evidence against every channel through which a binding wage floor reduces youth employment.

#### What the aggregate data show, and why they do not settle it

The national series cut both ways and are the weakest of the three kinds of evidence, because they contain no counterfactual.

In the window the thesis names, the aggregate evidence is against a large effect. By May 2019 — after Ontario's $14 and Alberta's $15 had both taken effect — youth employment was up 64,000 (+2.6%) year over year and the youth unemployment rate was 10.0%, and the employment rate for returning students aged 20 to 24 was "the highest rate for the month of May since 2008" [10]. Over 2019 as a whole, youth employment gains totalled 115,000 (+4.8%) and the youth unemployment rate reached an all-time low of 10.0% in May [6]. A policy that cut 23,000 youth jobs in one province, in a country where young people number in the millions, is compatible with those national numbers — Alberta is about 11 per cent of Canada's youth — but the national series cannot confirm or refute it.

The one aggregate signal that does point the thesis's way is sectoral. Employment in accommodation and food services had trended downward since May 2018, falling 63,000 (-5.0%) over the 12 months to May 2019 [10] — the most minimum-wage-intensive sector in the country, contracting in the year the largest increases landed. That is consistent with a wage-floor effect. It is equally consistent with a demand shift, a labour-supply shift, or the ordinary churn of a sector with high turnover, and no Canadian study has separated them for that period.

The deterioration that people now associate with youth job losses is a different event, in a different period. Statistics Canada dates it precisely: the youth employment rate had generally been on a strong downward trend following a recent high of 59.4% in March 2023, was down 2.4 percentage points year over year in May 2024, and sat below the 58.2% average of 2017–2019 [11]. The student unemployment rate climbed from a record low of 11.4% in May 2022 to 20.1% in May 2025 [2]. By then the minimum wage in most provinces was indexed to CPI and rising by a few per cent a year — real increases near zero.

#### What the crux resolves to

Weighing the three, the evidence supports a narrow, conditional version of the thesis and not the version as stated.

The Fossati–Marchand result is the strongest single piece of evidence: a large, unexpected, spatially patterned, placebo-tested youth-specific employment loss, of a magnitude consistent with the Canadian meta-analytic elasticity, in the one Canadian jurisdiction that ran the experiment the thesis describes. It should be weighted heavily because its identification is the best available and because the Kaitz index shows the treatment was strong enough to bite.

But it is one province, one episode, and — critically — it is an episode that began in 2015, before the 2017 date in the thesis. Alberta announced and started phasing in its increase in 2015, reaching $15 in October 2018. Ontario's comparable increase to $14 in January 2018 has not been subjected to a published synthetic-control study of the same quality that I could find. So the strongest evidence for the thesis is evidence about Alberta's 2015–2018 increase, and the thesis's 2017 date is approximately right for the completion of that increase and for Ontario's, but the causal episode is earlier than the framing implies.

Against it, Brochu et al. show that the layoff mechanism is absent in Canadian data over a long window of smaller changes. That does not refute Fossati and Marchand — different period, different size of treatment, different outcome measured — but it means the thesis cannot claim a well-established mechanism. It can claim an employment-level result whose mechanism is not yet demonstrated in Canadian microdata.

The crux, then, is the Kaitz index and what it implies about generalisation. Alberta's increase took the minimum to 92 per cent of the median youth wage. Ontario's took it to a level that, at $14 in 2018, was roughly 70 per cent of the median youth wage in that province — binding, but on a narrower slice of the youth distribution. The thesis as stated is about all provincial increases since 2017. The evidence supports an effect where the floor became binding on most young workers, and does not establish one where it did not. That is a real finding, and it is not the claim as written.

### 5. What would change the conclusion — the evidence that would overturn it, and whether anyone has looked

Four pieces of evidence would overturn or sharply qualify the conclusion. Two of them exist and have not been brought to bear; two do not exist and could be produced.

### 1. An Ontario study of the same quality as the Alberta one

This is the largest gap in the record. Ontario's minimum wage rose from $11.60 in 2017 to $14.00 on 1 January 2018 — a 20.7 per cent increase in a single step, in a province with roughly 40 per cent of Canada's population — and then was frozen at $14 by the incoming government, which cancelled the scheduled rise to $15. That cancellation is close to an ideal natural experiment: two provinces that both legislated a large increase, one of which then stopped. A difference-in-differences or synthetic-control design using Ontario as treated and the provinces that never legislated $15 as controls, with the cancellation as a separate test, would identify the effect of the largest single-step increase in the country. I found no published study of that design at the quality of Fossati and Marchand's. Until one exists, the thesis rests on one province, and the generalisation to "provincial minimum wages since 2017" is an extrapolation.

The Ontario case also has a feature that could cut against the thesis. Ontario has maintained a student sub-minimum throughout — currently $16.90 against a general rate of $17.95, applying to students under 18 working 28 hours a week or less [12] — and the 2018 increase raised the student rate alongside the general one. If the effect runs through the youngest workers, the sub-minimum partially shields them; if it runs through 20–24 year-olds, it does not. A well-designed Ontario study could separate these.

### 2. A study of whether the effect operates through hiring rather than separations

Brochu et al.'s finding that separations do not spike around minimum wage increases [9] is the sharpest challenge to the thesis's mechanism, but it addresses only one channel. The thesis would survive if the effect operates through reduced hiring: fewer entry-level positions created, fewer summer students taken on, more hours loaded onto existing staff. Nobody has tested that channel in Canadian data for a large increase.

This is testable and has not been tested. Firm-level payroll data — Statistics Canada's Survey of Employment, Payrolls and Hours, or the administrative payroll files Brochu et al. already use — could measure whether establishments in a province with a large increase reduced their headcount of young workers at the point of hiring, and whether they substituted hours for bodies. The distinction matters for policy: if the effect is on hiring, the workers who bear the cost are those who never got the job, and they are invisible in separation data and mostly invisible in the unemployment rate, because many of them never enter the labour force.

### 3. A post-2022 study, which nobody can yet write

The decline in youth employment that people actually point to is dated by Statistics Canada to March 2023 onward [11], with the returning-student unemployment rate rising from 11.4 per cent in May 2022 to 20.1 per cent in May 2025 [2]. Over that period the minimum wage in most provinces was indexed to CPI. A study of that episode would have to identify an effect from provincial variation in indexation formulas, which produce differences of a percentage point or two a year — far too small, on the Kaitz-index logic, to generate a movement of eight percentage points in student unemployment.

That is the thesis's deepest problem, and it is not one that further research can fix. The policy and the outcome are in different periods, and the policy was near-dormant in the period the outcome occurred. What research can do is measure how much of the 2022–2025 deterioration is attributable to labour supply growth and sectoral demand. The raw material exists: the returning-student population grew 10.2 per cent between May 2023 and May 2025 while student employment fell 1.6 per cent [7], and student employment in accommodation and food services fell 22.1 per cent year over year in May 2025 while employment in the other two main student industries was little changed [2]. A shift-share decomposition using pre-2022 industry employment shares would say how much of the student unemployment increase is composition — students concentrated in the one industry that collapsed — and how much is a genuine decline in job-finding within industries. As far as I can tell, no one has published that decomposition for Canada.

### 4. A youth-specific counterfactual for the 2017–2019 window

The Bank of Canada's 60,000-job projection is a model output, not an observation [1]. Nothing has tested it ex post. A study that took the Bank's own model, fed it the actual increases that occurred, and compared its predicted youth employment path with the realized path would tell us whether the model was right — and the answer matters for the thesis, because the 60,000 figure is the number most often cited in its support. If the model over-predicted, the thesis loses its most authoritative citation. If it was approximately right, the national series are consistent with a real but modest effect that is simply too small to see against the cycle.

#### What would not change the conclusion

Further studies of small, anticipated Canadian minimum wage changes would not move the verdict. The Canadian literature already contains many of them, and the meta-analytic elasticity of about -0.27 for teenagers [5] is drawn from exactly that variation. Adding more of the same variation will not tell us about a $15 floor at 92 per cent of the median youth wage, because that treatment is outside the range the literature observes. The disagreement is about large increases, and only studies of large increases can resolve it.

Similarly, further American evidence would not settle it. The Canadian Kaitz-index trajectory in Alberta — reaching 92 per cent for young workers [8] — has no close American analogue outside a handful of cities, and the institutional setting (a provincial minimum applying uniformly across urban and rural labour markets, with no tipped-credit offset for most workers) is different enough that U.S. elasticities do not transfer directly. Fossati and Marchand's own summary is that Canadian elasticities are typically larger than American ones, ranging from -0.17 to -0.75 [8].

#### Where this leaves the question

The thesis would be **confirmed** by an Ontario study finding a youth-specific employment loss around the January 2018 increase, with a pre-trend test and a cancellation-based robustness check, of a magnitude consistent with an elasticity near -0.15. It would be **refuted** by such a study finding no loss, or by a hiring-channel study showing that establishments absorbed large increases without reducing young headcount. It would be **substantially reinterpreted** — as it should be now — by accepting that the effect exists only where the floor binds on most of the youth wage distribution, which is a conditional claim about Alberta-scale increases rather than a claim about Canadian minimum wages in general.

The one thing that would not happen is the thesis being confirmed as written. Its date range is wrong for the outcome it is used to explain, its strongest evidence predates the date it names, and the Canadian microdata do not show the mechanism it requires. What survives is narrower and better supported: a large, rapid, unexpected provincial increase that took the minimum wage to more than 90 per cent of the median youth wage cost young Albertans roughly 23,000 jobs, and a smaller increase that binds on less of the distribution probably cost proportionally less — which is not the same as saying the increases since 2017 reduced youth employment across Canada.
